"Original Meaning and the Freedom of Speech and Press": "Ambiguous Evidence: Enjoining Repetition of Libels"

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1292 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Reason

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I'm serializing my fresh Notre Dame Law Review article, "Original Meaning and the Freedom of Speech and Press: Some Illustrative Examples"; here's the third and last Part:.
  • It has been revealed that throughout much of American history, the dominant view has been that courts can't enjoin libels.
  • Yet since then, many state courts have allowed permanent injunctions against libels.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I'm serializing my fresh Notre Dame Law Review article, "Original Meaning and the Freedom of Speech and Press: Some Illustrative Examples"; here's the third and last Part:.

It has been revealed that throughout much of American history, the dominant view has been that courts can't enjoin libels. The first precedent on this was Brandreth v. Lance (1839), an 1839 New York trial court decision. This was followed by State ex rel. Liversey v. Judge (1882), an 1882 Louisiana Supreme Court decision. Subsequent decisions helped establish this as a firm rule, seemingly culminating in Near v. Minnesota ex rel. Olson.

Yet since then, many state courts have allowed permanent injunctions against libels. By my count the court systems of thirty-four states have either so held or have in practice been so acting, with only six states plus D.C. continuing to categorically bar such injunctions. {See Eugene Volokh, Anti-Libel Injunctions, 168 U. Pa. L. Rev. 73 (2019).}.

This trend seems to have accelerated with the rise of the internet. Historically, a libel has been a short, sharp shock—typically, a one-time article in a newspaper that is printed and can't be removed—with the only possible remedy being damages or criminal prosecution. But the internet can turn libel into a steady drip, drip, drip of damage, with more readers seeing a libelous web page every day. Injunctions thus seem a more useful remedy.

Industry observers note that the internet also makes it easier for judgment-proof defendants to cause real damage; an injunction can thus be useful in a way that a damages remedy might not be. Criminal libel is theoretically available in about ten states, and there are indeed likely a couple of dozen criminal libel prosecutions in the United States each year. But in most states the only way to deploy criminal remedies in service of protecting reputation is through getting an injunction that can be enforced through the threat of criminal contempt.

Industry observers note that are these injunctions contrary to the original meaning of the First Amendment? The answer turns out to be complicated, especially if we focus on permanent injunctions, entered to forbid the repetition of material found to be libelous in a final judgment (with the defendant having had an opportunity to call for a jury trial).

It's true that early sources often view the freedom of the press as precluding prior restraints: To quote William Blackstone, "The liberty of the press is indeed essential to the nature of a free state: but this consists in laying no previous restraints upon publications, and not in freedom from censure for criminal matter when published." Yet this doesn't quite speak to the modern question whether the law may restrain repetition of material for matter found to be criminal (or tortious).

According to recent reports, nor does it speak to whether the law may require removal of such matter after a trial: Removal just wasn't practically an option in the print era. In such situations of injunctions against repetition of an already published libel or ordering its removal, "[e]very freeman" would retain the "undoubted right to lay what sentiments he pleases before the public" (again quoting Blackstone) at least in the first instance.

According to recent reports, nor is there a "restrictive power of a licenser" or "control of an inspector" in the sense that the Framers likely understood licensers, which is to say officials administering a licensing system. (To quote St. George Tucker, under that system "all books printed were previously licensed by some of the great offices of state, or the two universities, and all foreign books were exposed to a similar scrutiny before they were vended.") The injunction is imposed by a judge, often following a jury verdict, administering justice between two parties, not running a traditional licensing system that "subject[s] all freedom of sentiment to the prejudices of one man, and make[s] him the arbitrary and infallible judge of all controverted points in learning, religion, and government.".

According to recent reports, likewise, early sources stressed the importance of allowing a jury to resolve what is true and false in libel cases. But, as I noted, the modern permanent injunction in libel cases is entered after a final judgment on the merits, which at least in principle allows a defendant to demand a jury trial. If the defendant has so demanded, then any injunction would be based on the jury verdict.

This stems in part from the twentieth-century merger of law and equity, since equitable remedies, such as injunctions, can now be issued following the use of the legal procedure of a jury trial. (Historically, one argument against injunctions in libel cases has been that "equity will not enjoin a libel," a statement about the limits of the equity courts more than about constitutional protections for free expression.) Indeed, the Delaware Court of Chancery, which operates in a state system where law and equity remain largely separate, has continued to hold that it generally can't enjoin libel. But it expressly left open the possibility that, once the Delaware Superior Court (the law court) concludes—after a jury trial, if the parties don't choose a bench trial—that a statement is libelous, an injunction can then be issued.

Recent findings suggest that in practice, anti-libel injunctions are often parts of default judgments, or follow bench trials, and thus don't involve factual findings by juries. In both those situations, though, the defendant can be noted to have waived his right to a jury trial. To be sure, temporary restraining orders and preliminary injunctions are entered before any opportunity for a jury trial—but for that reason many courts continue to reject them on First Amendment grounds.

In a recent development, and, as the California Supreme Court held in allowing such post-final-judgment permanent injunctions, the reasoning of Near v. Minnesota ex rel. Olson expressly sets aside injunctions in traditional civil libel disputes:.

The high court was careful to point out … that the statute being considered was "not aimed at the redress of individual or private wrongs. Remedies for libel remain available and unaffected." … But most significant is that the court … clarified that it was not addressing "questions as to the extent of authority to prevent publications in order to protect private rights according to the principles governing the exercise of the jurisdiction of courts of equity." In a footnote, the court cited [an] … article by Roscoe Pound that observed that English courts permit "an injunction in case the libel was repeated or publication was continued after a jury had found the matter libelous." Therefore, Near expressly did not address the issue posed in the present case.

In a recent development, the Supreme Court hasn't confronted such permanent injunctions against repetition of proven libel since Near, but it has authorized injunctions against obscenity (which Near had anticipated) and against commercial speech that proposes illegal transactions. The one case in which it granted certiorari as to anti-libel injunctions, Tory v. Cochran (2005), largely disappeared when the plaintiff, famed lawyer Johnnie Cochran, died while the case was pending. None of these cases discussed the original meaning of the First Amendment, and the lower court cases dealing with the matter have largely not discussed it, either.

Sources indicate that so here we have a fairly rich body of originalist evidence related to libel law generally. We have a considerable body of evidence from before and shortly after the Framing that talks about "previous restraints." And we have some nineteenth-century sources that seem to take the view that all injunctions in libel cases are unconstitutional. But how exactly do the Framing-era sources apply to a permanent anti-libel injunction issued by a court following the resolution of a libel case? Hard to know for sure.

National Security Division Announces First “Near Miss” Non-Prosecution Agreement Under the Department-wide Corporate Enforcement Policy

📅 27 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (778 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fbi

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Department of Justice declared today that it has entered into a non-prosecution agreement with Extreme Networks, Inc.
  • The Department reached the agreement under its 2026 Corporate Enforcement and Voluntary Self-Disclosure Policy (“the Policy”), which incentivizes companies to voluntarily disclose discovered misconduct, cooperate with Department investigations, and timely and appropriately remediate the wrongdoing.
  • This agreement with Extreme Networks marks the Department’s first non-prosecution agreement in a “near-miss” case under the Policy, meaning a case that involved full cooperation and appropriate remediation but did not qualify for a declination of prosecution.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Department of Justice declared today that it has entered into a non-prosecution agreement with Extreme Networks, Inc. The company agreed to pay criminal penalties totaling $975,721.84 to resolve the Department’s investigation of sanctions and export control offenses.

The Department reached the agreement under its 2026 Corporate Enforcement and Voluntary Self-Disclosure Policy (“the Policy”), which incentivizes companies to voluntarily disclose discovered misconduct, cooperate with Department investigations, and timely and appropriately remediate the wrongdoing.

This agreement with Extreme Networks marks the Department’s first non-prosecution agreement in a “near-miss” case under the Policy, meaning a case that involved full cooperation and appropriate remediation but did not qualify for a declination of prosecution. While Extreme Networks’ disclosure to the National Security Division (NSD) was not timely because it occurred under imminent threat of disclosure by a news publication, Extreme Networks nonetheless fully cooperated with the Department’s investigation and timely and appropriately remediated the misconduct. As a result, its disclosure qualified as a “Near Miss” Voluntary Self-Disclosure under the Policy.

It has been revealed that “This non-prosecution agreement and million-dollar criminal penalty mark the successful resolution of our investigation into the illegal sale of advanced networking equipment and services to a Russian weapons manufacturer, in clear violation of U.S. sanctions and export controls,” noted Assistant Director Roman Rozhavsky of the FBI’s Counterintelligence and Espionage Division. “The FBI remains dedicated to keeping sensitive technology out of the hands of the Russian military, and we're grateful to Homeland Security Investigations and the Bureau of Industry and Security for their partnership on this case. Let this announcement serve as a clear warning: if you attempt to arm our adversaries by violating U.S. law, justice will find you.”.

It has been revealed that “HSI remains committed to investigating companies and individuals who evade U.S. export controls and sanctions to provide goods or services to foreign weapons manufacturers,” said Acting Special Agent in Charge Jeremy Pierczynski of Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) Detroit. “These laws protect our national security and prevent U.S.-origin products and services from supporting adversaries’ military capabilities. HSI will continue working with our law enforcement and regulatory partners to identify and hold accountable those who undermine these critical safeguards.”.

The agreement arose out of an investigation into Extreme Networks’ sales of products and services to Moscow Machinery Building Plant Avangard (MMZA), a Russian weapons manufacturer that was owned by JSC Concern Almaz-Antey (Almaz Antey), which was added to the Specially Designated Nationals and Blocked Persons List by the Department of the Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) in July 2014.

Pursuant to the non-prosecution agreement, Extreme Networks will forfeit $487,860.92 in proceeds from the sanctions and export control offenses and pay a criminal fine of $487,860.92, for a total criminal penalty of $975,721.84. Extreme Networks will also resolve a parallel administrative action by OFAC.

Between around March 2018 and March 2022, Extreme Networks, through its then-Russia based subsidiary, Extreme Networks Rus LLC, processed and fulfilled 11 purchase orders for networking equipment and services to MMZA without the required license or authorization from OFAC. MMZA was a primary producer of the S-300 and S-400 anti-aircraft missile systems used by the Russian army. To facilitate these sales, certain Russia-based Extreme Networks employees concealed the identity of MMZA from Extreme Networks’ global trade compliance group, causing Extreme Networks to file false electronic export information via the Automated Export System and smuggle goods from the United States. Through this scheme, Extreme Networks deprived the U.S. government of its ability to carry out its lawful function of enforcing sanctions and export controls designed to protect national security and economic interests. As a result of its unlawful conduct, Extreme Networks earned approximately $487,860.92 in revenue from the sales of goods and services.

Sources indicate that although Extreme Networks’ self-disclosure to NSD was not timely pursuant to the Policy, Extreme Networks nonetheless cooperated with the Department’s investigation by timely providing relevant facts and documents and making employees available for interviews. Extreme Networks also appropriately remediated the misconduct by terminating its contract with the third-party distributor it used to facilitate these sales, improving screening procedures, hiring additional compliance personnel, and implementing diligence procedures in connection with mergers and acquisitions. Given these steps and the lack of aggravating circumstances, the Department agreed to enter into a non-prosecution agreement.

The FBI Charlotte Field Office, the Department of Commerce’s Bureau of Industry and Security, and Homeland Security Investigations investigated the case.

This case was prosecuted by former Trial Attorney Maria Fedor of the National Security Division’s Counterintelligence and Export Control Section and Assistant U.S. Attorney Adam Hulbig for the Eastern District of North Carolina.

Please see the Justice Department’s policy here.

A combination square pairs a sliding ruler with a head for checking 90- and 45-degree angles, measuring depths, and marking consistent offsets. A combination square’s usefulness depends on the relationship between its blade and head. The blade should be straight, the graduations correctly spaced, and the working faces accurately set at 90 and 45 degrees. Fine scale divisions alone don’t establish accuracy; a detailed ruler cannot compensate for an out-of-square head.

Check a new square before relying on it. Register the head against a known straight edge, draw a fine line, then flip the square and draw again from the same point. Diverging lines indicate a problem. Keep contact surfaces free of debris, and repeat the check after a drop or impact that could affect alignment.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The motion arises from an altercation between respondent and participants in a demonstration outside of the federal courthouse for the Southern District of New York on September 29, 2025.
  • According to recent reports, on September 29, 2025, respondent, then 61 years old, was leaving a meeting at the Newly introduced York County District Attorney's Office and was walking toward the Brooklyn Bridge.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

From a N.Y. appellate decision Thursday in Att'y Grievance Comm. v. Fernich (Judges Sallie Manzanet-Daniels, Tanya R. Kennedy, Barbara R. Kapnick, Kelly O'Neill Levy, and Matthew Parker-Raso); the respondent, Marc Fernich, is a prominent Latest York criminal defense lawyer, who represented, among others, Jeffrey Epstein, John Gotti, and Joaquin Guzman (drug cartel leader El Chapo):.

The motion arises from an altercation between respondent and participants in a demonstration outside of the federal courthouse for the Southern District of New York on September 29, 2025. On May 27, 2026, the AGC served respondent with a notice and petition of charges alleging one charge of professional misconduct under Rules of Professional Misconduct (22 NYCRR 1200.0) rule 8.4(h), which prohibits conduct that adversely reflects on the lawyer's fitness as a lawyer. The parties have submitted a stipulation of facts, respondent's affidavit, and materials addressing aggravation and mitigation. Respondent admits to the stipulated misconduct, acknowledges the consequences of consenting to discipline, and agrees to a public censure.

According to recent reports, on September 29, 2025, respondent, then 61 years old, was leaving a meeting at the Newly introduced York County District Attorney's Office and was walking toward the Brooklyn Bridge. On Centre Street, he came upon a group of demonstrators in support of Palestine outside of the federal courthouse. Some demonstrators were singing and chanting, one played a guitar, and others held a banner reading "Jewish Artists for Palestine.".

According to recent reports, respondent attempted to make his way through a circle of demonstrators, and admits that physical contact occurred as he attempted to proceed. Respondent grabbed a demonstrator's arm, pushed and grabbed others while moving through the circle, and engaged in heated verbal confrontation. The cellphone recordings of the incident also show respondent holding a demonstrator from behind with his arms around the person's waist, with the demonstrator shouting at him to remove his arms, respondent pushing and grabbing others, and respondent holding another demonstrator from behind with his arms around the individual's neck.

Among other things, respondent's threatening and antisemitic remarks included "Back off me, Kapo, Kike, Jew Boy!," "You fucking animal, you're worse than a fucking Muslim!," "You should have been aborted," and "You should have been thrown into an oven, I'd throw you in if I could!" He also said that the demonstrators' grandparents should have died in the Holocaust, as well as other inflammatory remarks invoking violence. Respondent remained at the demonstration for approximately one hour, until it ended.

At his deposition, respondent maintained that the video depiction of the incident was a compilation of cellphone recordings made by several individuals and that they were out of sequence and out of context. He asserted that the confrontation had not been one-sided; demonstrators had been linking arms, blocking his way, pushing back, and squeezing his genitals.

Sources indicate that he also maintained that the recordings had purposefully omitted much of the physical contact and extreme anti-Israel and anti-Zionist rhetoric directed at him. Nonetheless, he recognized that the demonstrators had been exercising their constitutional rights to assemble and engage in free speech, and that his words and actions could not be justified. He was deeply ashamed of his conduct and expressed remorse.

Recent findings suggest that the parties have stipulated that respondent's misconduct is aggravated by his substantial experience in the practice of law. They have also stipulated to considerable mitigation. Respondent has no prior disciplinary history. The incident was unrelated to his representation of a client or the practice of law, and did not disrupt a court proceeding. Respondent self-reported his misconduct to the AGC through counsel, cooperated with the AGC investigation, voluntarily appeared for examination, accepted responsibility, and expressed remorse and embarrassment for his actions. Fifteen character references described respondent as being well-regarded in the community and having character traits of honesty, integrity, and trustworthiness.

The record further reflects that respondent was experiencing significant medical concerns at the time of the incident. He was recovering from a recent back surgery and experiencing significant pain, and had undergone emergency surgery for retinal tears shortly beforehand. He was also undergoing psychiatric treatment and taking medication for depression, anxiety, and ADHD. A report submitted by respondent's treating psychiatrist explains how the pain, emotional distress, and psychiatric symptoms respondent was experiencing may have contributed to his impaired judgment and agitation and, while respondent had been under his care for 13 years, he would never have expected him to engage in the kind of "angry and out-of-control conduct that he engaged in outside the Courthouse." Respondent, who has family in Israel, also maintains that the October 7, 2023 attacks in Israel affected him deeply and that his memory of those attacks caused his anger to boil over.

Under 22 NYCRR 1240.8(a)(5), the Court may resolve a disciplinary matter by consent where the submissions establish an admitted violation and an appropriate agreed-upon sanction. In support of the proposal for a public censure, the parties cite decisions imposing a censure for similarly offensive, abusive, and discriminatory remarks and other isolated misconduct (see e.g. Matter of Melogy, 233 AD3d 135 [1st Dept 2024]; Matter of Mukambetova, 204 AD3d 158 [1st Dept 2022]; Matter of Schlossberg, 192 AD3d 8 [1st Dept 2020]).

According to recent reports, respondent's use of antisemitic and threatening language, together with his physical aggression towards demonstrators, warrants public discipline. At the same time, the absence of a disciplinary history, the isolated nature of the incident, the medical and psychological circumstances, his cooperation, and his acceptance of responsibility supports the sanction jointly proposed. Public censure appropriately expresses the profession's condemnation of the relevant conduct while also recognizing the substantial mitigation.

Accordingly, the parties' joint motion for discipline by consent pursuant to 22 NYCRR 1240.8(a)(5) should be granted, … and respondent publicly censured….

Jorge Dopico and Raymond Vallejo represent the Committee.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mohamed Sabry Soliman, 46, of Colorado Springs, Colorado, pleaded guilty in federal court today to 12 hate crimes charges for using Molotov cocktails to attack members of the group Run for Their Lives and others.

As part of the plea agreement, Soliman admitted that on June 1, 2025, he lit and threw two Molotov cocktails into a gathering of the Boulder chapter of Run for Their Lives, a group that organized walks throughout the United States to raise awareness for hostages still held after the October 7, 2023, terrorist attacks in Israel. Soliman further admitted that he targeted the group because of the victims’ actual or perceived Israeli national origin and Jewish religion. The attack killed one person and caused permanent and life-threatening injuries to several others.

It has been revealed that “No one should be subjected to violence because of their religion or national origin,” noted Assistant Attorney General Harmeet K. Dhillon of the Justice Department’s Civil Rights Division. “With this plea, we hope to deliver a measure of justice to the victims and their families. The Civil Rights Division remains committed to vigorously prosecuting the perpetrators of bias-motivated violence.”.

In a recent development, “By his own admissions, Mohamed Soliman’s hateful attack on our neighbors in Boulder was antisemitic,” stated U.S. Attorney for the District of Colorado Peter McNeilly. “All Americans should feel free to pursue their faith and way of life without fear that doing so will put their personal safety at risk. Antisemitism erodes the common ties that bind our great nation together and there is no place for it in America. We are grateful for the trust and support of the victims and the Boulder community as we prosecuted this case.”.

“This individual conducted a despicable attack on people he believed to be Jewish or who support Israel, and with today’s plea he is admitting his guilt,” noted Assistant Director Jarod Brown of the FBI’s Counterterrorism Division. “The FBI is steadfast in our commitment to protect our communities and uphold the Constitution. We will continue to work with our Justice Department partners to ensure those who harm others or attempt to intimidate those expressing their personal views are held accountable.”.

Recent findings suggest that “The chaos inflicted by this defendant spread its seeds far beyond Pearl Street, Boulder, and Colorado,” noted Special Agent in Charge Amanda Koldjeski of the FBI Denver Field Office. “FBI Denver is proud of the role we played in this case alongside our partners in Boulder: We do not tolerate acts of hate and terror against our neighbors. We will continue to work to keep our community safe and seek justice for victims.”.

For nine of his hate crimes charges, Soliman faces a maximum penalty of life in prison, five years of supervised release, and a fine of up to $250,000. For the three other hate crimes charges, Soliman faces a maximum penalty of 50 years in prison to run consecutive to any other prison term, three years of supervised release, and a fine of up to $250,000. A federal district court judge will determine any sentence after considering the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and other statutory factors. A sentencing hearing is scheduled for Jan. 7, 2027.

The FBI Denver Field Office and the Boulder Police Department investigated the case.

It has been revealed that assistant U.S. Attorneys Melissa Basche and Daniel Pastor for the District of Colorado and Trial Attorneys Sarah Howard and Khalil Quinan of the Civil Rights Division’s Criminal Section are prosecuting the case.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Industry observers note that on May 14, 2022, a man motivated by heinous white supremacist ideologies he allegedly adopted due to content he viewed on social media carried out a mass shooting at a Buffalo grocery store, killing 10 and injuring three others.
  • Recent findings suggest that these appeals concern motions to dismiss plaintiffs' claims against several social media companies whose platforms the shooter allegedly used before committing this unspeakable act of violence.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

From the 4-judge unsigned majority opinion in Patterson v. Meta Platforms, Inc., decided today by N.Y.'s high court:.

Industry observers note that on May 14, 2022, a man motivated by heinous white supremacist ideologies he allegedly adopted due to content he viewed on social media carried out a mass shooting at a Buffalo grocery store, killing 10 and injuring three others. Plaintiffs, victims of the shooting and their family members, commenced these actions against the shooter's parents, firearms manufacturers, and social media companies, seeking compensation for their injuries.

Recent findings suggest that these appeals concern motions to dismiss plaintiffs' claims against several social media companies whose platforms the shooter allegedly used before committing this unspeakable act of violence. Specifically, plaintiffs contend that their complaints state causes of action for products liability based on defective features of these social media defendants' platforms and their failure to warn thereof….

According to recent reports, [P]laintiffs failed to adequately plead that features of [the] social media defendants' products proximately caused their injuries. Generally, a defendant's acts qualify as a proximate cause when they are "a substantial cause of the events which produced the injury." This inquiry examines.

"the foreseeability of the event resulting in injury; the passage of time between the originally negligent act and the intervening act; the spatial gap, if any, between the original act and the intervening act; whether the original act of negligence was a completed occurrence or was ongoing at the time of the intervening act; whether and, if so, what other forces combined to bring about the harm; as well as public policy considerations regarding the scope of liability.".

Sources indicate that foreseeability is often the most significant factor. Indeed, if an unforeseeable intervening criminal act of a third party causes the plaintiff's injury, the causal connection is severed. Thus, proximate causation will not be found when the intervening act "is extraordinary under the circumstances, not foreseeable in the normal course of events, or independent of or far removed from the defendant's conduct." "Although foreseeability and proximate cause are generally questions for the factfinder, there are instances in which proximate cause can be determined as a matter of law because 'only one conclusion may be drawn from the established facts'" such as when "the original negligent act merely 'furnished the occasion for'—but did not cause—'an unrelated act to cause injuries not ordinarily anticipated.'".

Here, plaintiffs failed to adequately allege that the remaining social media defendants' product defects proximately caused the shooter to carry out the mass shooting that resulted in plaintiffs' injuries. The complaints, even accepting the factual allegations as true, fail to establish that the shooter's actions were a natural and foreseeable consequence of these defendants' decisions about how to design and operate their platforms.

In a recent development, instead, under the circumstances, the shooter's actions were so extraordinary as to sever the causal chain as a matter of law. {Our conclusion is limited to the unusual facts of this case, where the platforms' assertedly addictive features were alleged to have harmed the shooter rather than the plaintiffs directly.} We therefore need not address the scope of section 230 of the Communications Decency Act or how it would apply to the claims against these defendants.

Judge Halligan joined the majority, but also wrote a concurring opinion:.

I join the majority because I agree that the plaintiffs have not adequately pleaded proximate causation. I write separately to underscore that, for me, this conclusion rests squarely on the highly unusual facts presented here, and to offer some additional thoughts regarding the scope of section 230.

As an initial matter, I agree with my dissenting colleagues that the plaintiffs alleged that several of the defendants tortiously designed addictive products. The complaints make a number of general claims about social media and youth: that defendants' platforms are addictive; that compulsive use of social media, particularly by young people, causes emotional disturbance and "impulsive decision-making and risk-taking behavior"; and that such use can also yield other deleterious consequences, including "sleep disturbances, mental health problems and suicidal ideation, and violent, hateful acts." The complaints further assert that the social media defendants, knowing of the addictive quality of their products and the heightened susceptibility of young owners, not only failed to implement features for limiting use or warning parents, but also took deliberate advantage of that vulnerability by utilizing "strategic timing and clustering of notifications to lure back users" and by implementing "barriers to the deactivation and deletion of accounts." ….

I find the claims before us quite distinct from the cases cited by the dissent that have allowed products liability claims premised on the addictiveness of social media platforms to proceed. I have little doubt that a plaintiff could allege a sufficient connection between the design of a platform and adverse consequences for the mental health of young owners. In those cases, the harms that form the basis for the claims—for example, the alleged inducement of "compulsive use among young users to the detriment of their health and well-being"—flow directly from the platforms' allegedly defective features, leaving little question "that the defective design was a substantial factor in causing plaintiff's injury.".

Industry observers note that but the plaintiffs here are not bringing a claim on behalf of owners. Instead, they are seeking recompense for the victims of a crime committed by a social media user. In other words, the allegedly addictive properties of the platforms were not alleged to have harmed the plaintiffs here directly, but rather to have harmed the shooter, who in turn engaged in extensive research and planning before murdering ten people and wounding others…. I do not see the connection between the two as sufficiently articulated to allow the case to proceed.

Three aspects of these claims inform my conclusion. First, although intervening criminal acts do not necessarily sever the causal chain, the shooter's conduct was apparently painstakingly planned and extraordinarily violent.

Second, the prominence of content in many of plaintiffs' allegations gives me real pause. Even if we were to interpret section 230 as not immunizing defendants against claims for actions that rest, at least in part, on content, I am not aware of other instances where a court has held that provocative content proximately caused someone to commit a violent crime, and I am hesitant to take that step here. {I understand the plaintiffs to disclaim on appeal any effort to base liability on defendants' roles as publishers of content. But their complaints can be read to allege that the platforms are defective at least in part because of the racist and extremist content they make available, and the plaintiffs acknowledge that content is a necessary link in the causal chain leading to their harms.}.

Industry observers note that third, the defendants' platforms have billions of worldwide users. To the extent that proximate cause could rest on a correlation between social media use and a specific type of harmful act committed by any one of those users, the potential liability would sweep broadly, to say the least. If all such conduct were "a natural and foreseeable consequence" of a platform's design choices, the concept of proximate cause would have little meaning….

As for section 230, …. "we [have] read section 230 to bar 'lawsuits seeking to hold a service provider liable for its exercise of a publisher's traditional editorial functions.'" … Our endorsement of a "traditional editorial functions" test for section 230 immunity, however, does little to answer whether the conduct of modern social media platforms can be labelled such a function.

As to claims that a defendant designed its platform features to encourage or facilitate addiction, irrespective of the particular content promoted by the platform, I agree with the dissent that they are not barred by section 230. That is because such conduct does not constitute a traditional editorial function, even under a broad understanding of that term.

Recent findings suggest that as to claims that challenge a social media platform's use of content-recommendation algorithms, the dissent appears to take the view that content-recommendation algorithms which are designed to be addictive are not covered by section 230 immunity, since they increase engagement in a way that could not have been envisioned at the time that provision was enacted in 1996. I have no quarrel with how we framed the scope of section 230 in Shiamili: the key question is whether a platform engaged in a traditional editorial function, akin to a decision "to publish, withdraw, postpone or alter content." But whether platforms' use of content-recommendation algorithms can be remarked to resemble traditional decisions to publish, withdraw, postpone, or alter content is, for me, a more difficult question….

Sources indicate that [O]verly broad interpretations of section 230 in the face of a rapidly changing technological landscape are unmoored from Congress's purpose in enacting that provision—to protect minors from being exposed to pornography online…. Given that caution, I would not be inclined to extend section 230's reach to all content-recommendation algorithms. I am particularly skeptical that use of individualized content-recommendation algorithms—that is, algorithms that "assess[ ] a user's prior posts, friends, or viewing habits to recommend newly introduced content and connections"—constitutes a traditional publisher function. After all, "[t]raditional publication has never included selecting the news, opinion pieces, or classified ads to send to each individual reader based on guesses as to their preferences and interests." Instead, such functions may be "more analogous to the actions of a direct marketer, matchmaker, or recruiter than to those of a publisher.".

In my view, a closer question is presented as to engagement-maximizing algorithms that, unlike the algorithms described above, do not take into account any individual user's conduct but instead seek to "promote[ ] third-party content" based on "cumulative user engagement." On one hand, algorithms that do not respond to individual user conduct may be thought to resemble a publisher's traditional aim of presenting content that users, on the whole, want to see. On the other hand, one might conclude that "generic" content-based algorithms bear no more resemblance to traditional publication than their "'advanced'—individualized—counterparts" because they still rely on an assessment of user viewing habits in a manner akin to "a direct marketer" rather than a traditional publisher. My dissenting colleagues offer yet another variation on this point; they assert that engagement-maximizing algorithms differ from an editor's choice of where to place a news story because the algorithms are "designed to prey on neurological frailties and alter brain chemistry.".

In a recent development, whether section 230 protects any of these algorithms is, for me, a difficult question, and I do not think the record before us sheds much light on how different types of content-recommendation algorithms actually operate on the social media defendants' individual platforms—information that might affect my view. We need not decide those questions today because, whatever the scope of the "traditional editorial functions" protected by section 230, the plaintiffs have failed to sufficiently allege that the defendants' platforms' features caused their grave injuries.

Judge Rivera, joined by Chief Judge Wilson and Judge Troutman, dissented in relevant part; an excerpt from the very long opinion:.

Sources indicate that the complaints detail the shooter's transformation from a seemingly ordinary teenager into a virulent racist and violent white supremacist…. [In his manifesto, t]he shooter also wrote that he "was not born racist nor [did he] gr[o]w up to be racist." Rather, he was exposed to and indoctrinated in his ideology of racial violence after using various social media platforms, starting with Instagram, YouTube, and Snapchat in his early teen years, before he transitioned to more niche platforms like Reddit, Discord, Twitch and 4chan. The shooter claimed he rapidly "became transfixed with and addicted to [the] online world." He wrote in his diary:.

"I'm addict[ed] to consoooooming. It's 2 in the morning. w[hat] t[he] f[*ck] … I'll admit my mental health has seriously degraded these past few years, especially in the last few months. I should be sleeping right now. I'm just browsing online:/" (emphasis added).

According to recent reports, by his own account, he sacrificed "years of [his] life" to being online, often "stay[ing] up late" "browsing Reddit or watching YouTube" "every day." He stated that his compulsive social media use "seriously degraded" his mental health and isolated him from his peers. Rather than "go[ing] to friend's houses" or other social gatherings, "[e]very day after school [he] would just go home and play games and watch YouTube, mostly by [him]self." Ultimately, as he descended further into isolation, he believed he had no other choice but to commit this barbarous act.

In a recent development, plaintiffs allege that the shooter's experience of compulsive social media engagement is widespread because the products' addictive features are fundamental to the social media defendants' business model. According to plaintiffs, defendants' business models seek to maximize user engagement through products "designed to be addictive." Plaintiffs assert that the operation of these products on the shooter, and their adverse impact on his mind caused by their addictive features, are links in the proximate causal chain underlying plaintiffs' tort liability causes of action against the social media defendants….

Industry observers note that the Appellate Division erroneously concluded that defendants are immune from plaintiffs' lawsuit under Section 230. As I discuss, Section 230 does not shield defendants from plaintiffs' products liability and failure to warn allegations grounded on allegedly addictive products, as those claims have nothing to do with defendants' role as a third-party content publisher or as the creator of protected speech….

To the extent plaintiffs' claims against the social media defendants are based upon defendants' publication of third-party content, including racist, white supremacist, and violent content, defendants are immune from suit pursuant to Section 230. However, not all claims asserted in the complaints are based upon defendants' publication of third-party content. Rather, as I explain, the complaints also stated causes of action based on defendants' design of allegedly defective products and failure to warn….

Plaintiffs assert that these defendants are civilly liable for their role in addicting the shooter to social media and consequent deterioration of his mental health. Plaintiffs' complaints set forth the entire chain of causation that allegedly led to the mass shooting. By designing highly addictive algorithms known to cause severe mental harm to teenagers—like the shooter—the social media defendants created a direct link to the resulting damages, particularly given their failure to warn users and parents of these risks…. [T]here is no Section 230 immunity that attaches to the architecture of defendants' social media products—particularly their purposefully addictive algorithms….

In a recent development, defendants' alternative argument that the complaints were properly dismissed on First Amendment grounds is unpersuasive. At this pre-answer stage of the litigation, it is unclear how precisely the content-recommendation algorithms function, meaning it is not possible to determine, as a matter of law, on a motion to dismiss that the algorithms themselves are protected speech. That determination requires factual findings dependent on future discovery. On a motion to dismiss we only decide whether the plaintiffs' claim is cognizable and not whether it will eventually succeed based on the facts established by the record….

And here's a short excerpt from the dissent's long discussion of why it rejects the majority's proximate cause theory:.

The majority's conclusion that plaintiffs "fail to establish that the shooter's actions were a natural and foreseeable consequence" of the social media defendants' platforms because "the shooter's actions were so extraordinary as to sever the causal chain as a matter of law" is unsupported by our well-established tort liability doctrines. First, we have made clear that there may be more than one link in a causal chain and there may be more than one tortfeasor liable, jointly or individually, for a plaintiff's injuries. "[T]he mere fact that other persons share some responsibility for [the] plaintiff's harm does not absolve [a] defendant from liability." Thus, the fact that the third-party content creators may bear responsibility for the harm does not mean that defendants bear none.

In a recent development, second, a defect need only be a "substantial cause"—not the sole cause—"of the events which produced the injury." Substantial means more than slight or trivial. Plaintiffs' allegations that defendants' product adversely affected the shooter's mental health and behavior, making him a compulsive social media user, with the attendant negative impact on his mind and body, isolated from others, rendering him more susceptible to commit this horrific violent act, easily satisfies the "substantial cause" standard.

According to recent reports, third, not all intervening acts break the causal chain. An intervening act only breaks the causal nexus if it is extraordinary under the circumstances, unforeseeable in the normal course of events, or independent of and far removed from the defendant's conduct. That determination depends on whether the intervening act and its consequences were the foreseeable result of a defendant's tortious conduct. Even the "intentional" or "criminal" intervening acts of a third party can be reasonably foreseeable….

[W]hile here, the harm arose from exposure to graphic violence and white supremacist propaganda, plaintiffs allege that the algorithm is content-agnostic. According to plaintiffs, defendants' products and platforms rely on these complex algorithms to keep people engaged, which negatively impacts young people's mental health, and, in turn, increases the tendency to violent behavior, all the while driving revenue for these defendants. Thus, the majority's assertion that the shooter's actions were not foreseeable is nothing more than a factual conclusion, but that determination cannot be made by the Court on a motion to dismiss….

During a power outage, a generator that runs on gasoline can provide enough juice to keep your lights on, your groceries from spoiling, and your fans spinning. Set up a portable unit outside your home, and connect appliances inside to its numerous outlets via extension cords. Exactly how many appliances it’ll power at once depends on the wattage that generator can handle.

While a portable generator might cost several hundred or even thousands of dollars depending on size and model, when compared to a standby generator, which would kick on automatically to power your home, it’s certainly less expensive. Plus, you may not need a professional electrician to install a portable generator, and you can easily take the unit with you should you move. All that stated, proper operation of the machine is crucial to ensure the safety of your family and your community.

Before you start up a portable generator, bear in mind these two essential considerations:.

According to recent reports, WEN’s 5600-watt generator has a push-button start and is powerful enough to run household essentials; noise level is about 88 dB. Read the review.

Because portable gas generators emit carbon monoxide while they’re running and for some time afterward, positioning the generator properly and practicing careful carbon monoxide safety is critical.

Industry observers note that before you start up the generator, check the fuel gauge and fill the tank with gasoline as needed. (Make sure the generator is on a level surface to get an accurate reading on the fuel gauge.) If you need to add fuel, consult the owner’s manual for fuel requirements.

Next, check the oil level, which is like checking the oil in your car. Locate the oil dipstick (often below a removable maintenance panel). Pull out the dipstick, wipe it off, and then re-insert it. Carefully pull the dipstick straight out once more, then look to see if the oil on the stick falls between the lower and upper limit marks imprinted on the dipstick. Add or change the oil if necessary, referring to your owner’s manual for how to add, what kind to use, and how frequently it needs to be changed.

Recent findings suggest that before plugging in, ensure that you won’t overload the generator by connecting more appliances and lights than it is rated to handle. Add up the starting and running wattage of the appliances you want to power simultaneously; refer to their respective user manuals or check the backs or sides of the machines to find this information. The total number should not exceed the wattage limitations of your generator. Check your user’s manual if you’re unsure of how many watts of power your generator can handle. Stagger the use of appliances if necessary to prevent overloading the generator.

Follow your user manual for instructions on turning on the machine. You typically will need to turn the circuit breaker off and turn the fuel valve on before starting it up. Give the machine a few minutes to warm up, then flip the circuit breaker on.

Sources indicate that use long, heavy-duty extension cords made for outdoor use to connect appliances to the generator one by one so as not to overload it. Examine cords before use to ensure they are in good condition with no rips or tears. The cord’s wattage rating should be greater than the wattage of what you’ve plugged into it.

Industry observers note that to shut down the generator, turn off or disconnect the appliances plugged into it. Then refer to your user’s manual to power down the generator—typically you’ll need to turn the circuit breaker, engine switch, and fuel valve to the “off” position.

Recent findings suggest that wait until the generator is completely cooled down before storing it once power is restored. If you don’t anticipate needing it again for more than a month, drain the fuel and carburetor. Leaving old fuel can damage the generator’s internal parts. Refer to your owner’s manual for storage instructions.

Industry observers note that when running a portable generator, safety is the name of the game. Keep these tips in mind before, during, and after use.

Maintaining healthy indoor air quality is essential for protecting members of your household from hidden carcinogens, allergens, and harmful particulates. Pollutants can enter your living space from a range of sources, including building materials that emit volatile organic compounds (VOCs) and poor ventilation that traps moisture and encourages mold growth.

While clues like window condensation, musty odors, or unexplained respiratory symptoms can signal trouble, invisible, odorless threats such as radon and carbon monoxide often go undetected without the right equipment. We spoke to indoor air quality experts to identify the top five indoor air pollutants in U.S. homes and how to fix or mitigate them.

This monitor impressed our product testers with accurate readings, and it connects to an app where consumers can find air quality reports for their home.

In a recent development, particulate matter—including tiny airborne particles like pollen, smoke, soot, and other debris—is one of the most common indoor air pollutants, states Dr. Jaspreet Dhau, an expert on indoor air quality and purification and vice president of research and development at Molekule in Palm Beach Gardens, Florida. “Fine particulate matter, particularly PM2.5, which is a particle measuring 2.5 microns [micrometers] or smaller, is a concern because it can travel deep into the respiratory system,” says Dhau. Common sources include cooking, burning candles, using a fireplace, vacuuming, and even opening windows when outdoor pollution levels are high.

According to recent reports, VOCs are gases released by certain household products and materials such as paint, solvents, flooring, furniture, adhesives, cleaning supplies, air fresheners, and personal care products. “VOC levels may be higher during and after a home renovation, when new furniture is brought into a home, or when products containing chemical ingredients are used without adequate ventilation,” says Dhau. For example, certain pressed wood furniture and building materials can release formaldehyde, he explains.

Carbon monoxide (CO) is a combustion byproduct, a pollutant released when something burns. “In a typical home, sources can include gas stoves, fireplaces, wood-burning stoves, furnaces, water heaters, candles, and tobacco products,” says Dhau. “Carbon monoxide is especially dangerous because it’s colorless and odorless, making it difficult to detect without a working CO alarm.”.

Biological contaminants such as dust mites and pet dander are airborne pollutants that originate from living organisms, says Dhau. “Dust mites are a frequent problem and tend to collect in mattresses, carpets, upholstered furniture, and bedding. They can enter homes through open windows, pets, clothing, and HVAC systems,” he explains. Signs you might have a problem include frequent dust buildup on surfaces, allergy symptoms, excess pet hair and dander, and dust accumulating around air vents, adds Bill Myers, indoor air quality expert and group manager for technical sales at Panasonic Eco Systems North America.

Quiet, effective and easy to use, this commercial-grade unit cleans the air with a washable pre-filter, a carbon filter, and a HEPA filter.

In a recent development, everyday activities such as cooking and showering introduce moisture into the home. “When excess moisture is not adequately removed, particularly in bathrooms, basements, and other low-ventilation areas, conditions can become more favorable for mold and mildew growth,” notes Meyers. You might notice foggy mirrors that take a long time to clear, condensation on windows, musty odors, bathrooms that remain damp long after use, and visible mold or mildew.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that we may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›.

According to recent reports, power outages are top of mind now more than ever before—and for good reason. One in four households experience a power outage in a year, according to U.S. Census Bureau data, and 70 percent of those reporting outages were without power for 6 hours or more. These longer outages are not only disruptive; they can also be expensive, considering that the U.S. Food and Drug Administration recommends tossing perishable food kept in the refrigerator after just 4 hours without power.

Backup power promises comfort and security, which is why so many homes rely on a portable generator or power station. That category has grown from gas-powered generators to multi-fuel units, portable power stations, and whole-home batteries. The newest member of the family? A fridge backup.

It has been revealed that just in 2026, this new style hard-introduced with models from three industry leaders: Bluetti’s Fridge Power, Jackery’s FridgeGuard, and Backup Core by BioLite. And the consumer response has been powerful. Bluetti’s Kickstarter hit 145 percent of its funding goal in 45 days. Jackery debuted as a Costco exclusive in June and expanded its retail distribution after hearing about customers carrying home multiple units. BioLite has released its Backup in two waves already, each selling out in weeks, and is taking orders now for January shipments. Clearly, homeowners want a backup built just for the fridge. Keep reading to learn more about what sets fridge backups apart and when one beats a generator.

Fridge-optimized batteries all share three main hallmarks:.

Think of it like a larger version of the uninterruptible power supply (UPS) that you might use in a home office or with a high-end entertainment center to keep your connected electronics running during a brownout or blackout. A UPS in the home office might offer surge protection and enough battery life to run your computer for another 5 minutes so you can safely shut it down; this fridge-optimized backup can keep your most important kitchen appliance on for 15 hours or more.

And while we call them “fridge” backups, the design is actually much more versatile. Plug them in and slip the slim backups easily into any room to keep an vital appliance operational for hours: under a bed to power a CPAP machine, behind a bookshelf within cord’s reach of an air purifier, or behind the fish tank to maintain the family pet’s habitat.

Kickstarter backers for the Backup by BioLite—which first debuted in 2024 on the crowdfunding platform—“got it” immediately. “They understood the problem it was solving, and most questions revolved around understanding additional applications and setups beyond the fridge because the kitchen application was so intuitive,” indicates Erica Rosen, the VP of Marketing at BioLite and Goal Zero brands. “For example, we got a lot of questions about sump pumps and if Backup could run one during an outage.” (Spoiler alert: It can.).

Today, homeowners (and renters!) have many options for backup power, each with its own set of pros and cons.

A standby generator or whole-home battery backup automatically kicks in to keep the essentials—if not the whole home—running during an outage. Each type of backup connects at the electrical panel with a transfer switch. As such, each is a larger investment (read: more expensive) and a permanent installation that requires a licensed electrician. These backups also require forethought about fuel. A standby generator will require a source of liquid propane and/or natural gas, whereas whole-home batteries are often charged from the grid before an event and potentially recharged via solar panels when the grid is down.

According to recent reports, A portable gas-powered generator is more affordable than a standby option, but should only be run outdoors, which creates some limitations. For starters, you need to be home to turn a portable generator on and connect to your appliance. Then, you’ll need a long, heavy-duty outdoor-rated extension cord to reach the kitchen. These generators operate loudly, emit exhaust fumes, and require you to store enough fuel to be ready for the worst. Assuming you have a good supply, though, you can keep your appliance(s) powered with minimal interruption using a reliable portable generator.

A power station brings backup power indoors to power multiple electronics and small appliances. Power stations are the closest comparison. They are safe to use indoors or out and feature similar battery capacities. You can find options in the ballpark of 1 to 2 kWh for similar price points. They can, but may not always be, plugged in 100 percent of the time to act as a UPS. And importantly, they’re often too bulky to leave out next to a refrigerator 24/7.

It has been revealed that A fridge backup offers instant power backup without a permanent installation. It’s ideal for the consumer who is looking for a user-friendly, set-and-forget setup and a safety net that offers enough power to keep a fridge running for approximately 15 hours while the power is out—longer if additional batteries are connected.

“It’s [designed for] someone who wants peace of mind without having to think too much about backup power. Maybe you live somewhere with frequent storms, or you’ve come home after an outage to find everything in your freezer has spoiled,” says Beau Tyrrel, Product Manager at Jackery. “It’s also useful for renters and those who live in apartments and can’t install a whole-home backup system. All you need is a standard outlet, and you can take it with you when you move.”.

Sources indicate that the design is appealing in more ways than one, notes Luna Yan, affiliate marketing manager at Bluetti. A fridge backup solves spatial problems that come with more traditional portable power stations: “Traditional backup power systems are often bulky, making them difficult to accommodate in homes with limited space, particularly in kitchens and apartments.”.

In a recent development, “When we set out to develop Backup, we knew the world didn’t need another box-format power station. We did a lot of user research and found that there was a meaningful gap between the power stations of the world and expensive whole-home backup solutions, and it was leaving a lot of people out of the resiliency conversation,” Rosen notes. “As we explored ways to answer this, it became clear that form factor was going to be a really notable element: If we wanted something plugged in permanently to enable automatic performance, it needed to be really easy and it could not take up precious living space.”.

Recent findings suggest that it’s especially useful if you’re away when the power goes out and can’t move the fridge’s plug to a generator. Already plugged into the wall from setup, the backup’s stored power will be usable immediately. Each model’s mobile app indicates outage alerts, battery level, and power draw from anywhere.

In a recent development, “[A fridge backup is] also useful for renters and those who live in apartments and can’t install a whole-home backup system. All you need is a standard outlet, and you can take it with you when you move.”.

There’s a cost to every power outage. One of the biggest concerns for most homeowners is the spoiled food in a refrigerator after 4 hours without power. “Refrigerators are one of the few appliances in your home that needs to run around the clock,” Tyrrel claims. “When the power goes out, you could lose hundreds of dollars in groceries.”.

It has been revealed that A blackout can cost the average American household $117 in spoiled groceries, according to a survey of more than 1,000 Americans by the Texas electric provider Payless Power. One in five homes had it worse, losing more than $200 in groceries during a single outage.

According to recent reports, using that average, we estimate that a $1,000 fridge backup pays for itself after 10 blackouts—potentially sooner in larger households or homes with especially packed fridges and freezers. For an area that experiences one to two extended blackouts in a year, this investment could earn its keep in as soon as 6 years—and these newly introduced backups are rated for 10 or more years of use.

Industry observers note that “Based on customer feedback, refrigerators are among the most notable appliances to keep running during a power outage,” Yan says. And for good reason: “Continuous refrigeration helps protect food, medications, and other temperature-sensitive items.”.

According to recent reports, if your utility firm offers a Time-of-Use (TOU) electricity pricing plan, any of these fridge backups can help you take advantage of the savings. TOU programs charge different supply rates based on when you use electricity, incentivizing customers to use more electricity when overall demand is low by charging less per kilowatt-hour (kWh) used. These “off-peak hours” vary by plan, but typically are overnight and early morning.

For the average homeowner, the main way to save on these plans is to optimize the electricity usage you can schedule: when you charge an electric vehicle, run the dishwasher, and wash or dry a load of laundry. A fridge, of course, runs all day, and an efficient, Energy Star-certified model can use anywhere from 358 kWh for a compact top-freezer unit to 805 kWh per year for a large side-by-side refrigerator. You can’t optimize the always-on appliance without either a whole-home power bank that recharges in an off-peak hour for use during peak times or, now, a fridge backup. In a connected mobile app, consumers specify the best times to charge (off-peak hours) and discharge (peak hours), effectively shifting the fridge’s grid use to cheaper hours.

Especially now, with rising concern about grid stability and the increasing frequency of natural disaster events that disrupt power, demand for energy backups is high. Each of these energy brands has sold out and replenished stock at least once already this year. So while you may be eager to set up your home with the first available fridge backup, here’s a comprehensive look at unit specs to help find the model best suited to your space and needs.

According to recent reports, bluetti’s fridge backup offers the largest base capacity—nearly double that of Jackery FridgeGuard, and expandable to 8 kWh (second only to BioLite’s 10.5 kWh). Divide the total cost by the capacity, and you’re paying about $470 per kWh, which is the most backup per dollar. One unit can power the typical modern fridge for 21 to 48 hours, and a maximized setup of FridgePower plus three BlueCell battery packs can power your fridge for 4 days. (Run time, of course, depends on the specific refrigerator’s energy consumption and usage conditions.) That makes the slim design even more impressive—though at 43 pounds, it’s a two-person job to wall-mount.

It has been revealed that the mobile app provides battery levels, outage status, and charging progress, plus a place to choose among four UPS modes: Standard, PV Priority (which prioritizes solar power), TOU (Time-of-Use), and Custom. It even tracks local weather, alerts you when a storm approaches, and switches to fast charging if needed. An optional magnetic display (sold separately) provides at-a-glance information including percentage charged, energy output, and UPS modes—all without opening your phone.

Recent findings suggest that on paper, the Jackery fridge backup appears to be the unit most specialized for fridge use. It offers up to 15 hours of power in the slimmest profile. One outlet (for the fridge) and a single expansion option make it the least flexible of the three—but if the fridge is all you need, it’s a perfect fit. It’s effective, affordable, lasts up to 16 years, and takes only one person to install the lightweight unit on a wall mount (sold separately). It offers surge protection for your most notable household appliance during voltage spikes and enough power to start the fridge.

According to recent reports, one distinction Jackery has over its competition is a choice between instant backup UPS and a delayed start. “Your refrigerator’s compressor needs a little time to recover,” Tyrrel explains. “When it stops, refrigerant pressure remains high on one side of the system. Restarting too quickly makes the motor work harder and briefly draw several times its normal current. Delayed Start gives the compressor a short pause before restarting, helping avoid unnecessary strain when power flickers on and off.”.

Recent findings suggest that from the moment an outage occurs, Backup Core automatically powers a refrigerator for 15 to 30 hours. At 29 inches long, it’s 5 to 6 inches longer than all of the other units, but rotating it can fit one atop even a fridge and its slim design should still slip behind the appliance on its vertical wall mount.

Given its size and expansion capabilities, it should come as no surprise that Backup Core also includes the most outlets for electronics. Whereas another model includes one or two ports on the unit, the forward-thinking BioLite design provides its own power strip—that’s three more openings for small kitchen appliances or other electronics to easily connect.

It has been revealed that bioLite’s Backup Core is a 1.5 kWh solution, similar to its sister brand Goal Zero Yeti 1500 (6th generation). “However, Backup can expand in 1.5kWh increments with the ‘Extend’ model, and chain up to 10.5kWh of localized capacity,” Rosen explains. That’s even more than the combined 8kWh capacity of the Yeti Pro 4000 and Yeti Pro Tank 4000. So while Backup Core is the priciest of the three, it’s also the only one that can grow into something close to a whole-home battery. Think of it less as a fridge backup and more as the first piece of a backup system.

Sources indicate that james Thomas Ashbacher, 37, of Spring Lake, North Carolina, a former U.S. government contractor, was arrested by the FBI on Tuesday for allegedly leaking national defense information by posting the information on a popular social media site, unlawfully retaining other national defense information at his residence, and stealing night vision goggles from the U.S. Army’s Special Operations Command.

According to the indictment, beginning in or about 2021, the defendant worked as an employee of a private organization that provided security and emergency management services at the U.S. Army Special Operations Command facility in Fort Bragg, North Carolina. To perform the required functions of his employment, Ashbacher held a Top Secret security clearance with Sensitive Compartmented Information (SCI) access.

As further detailed in the indictment, Ashbacher photographed and removed without authorization videos and photographs containing images of classified military operations and transmitted the materials to a social media site. The classified materials were later re-posted by other users to a second social media site. Ashbacher asked a social media user in a private message to remove some materials and further stated that he was “trying to do some damage control.” A search of Ashbacher’s residence also revealed a classified award write-up that contained additional national defense information, along with a night vision goggle system specific to a military unit within Army Special Operations Command that had been reported missing.

The FBI Charlotte Field Office is investigating the case with substantial assistance from the U.S. Department of the Army’s Criminal Investigative Division.

In a recent development, trial Attorney Leslie Esbrook of the National Security Division’s Counterintelligence and Export Control Section and Assistant U.S. Attorney Logan Liles for the Eastern District of North Carolina are prosecuting the case.

Industry observers note that an indictment is merely an allegation. All defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law.

We selected and tested a diverse assortment of waterproof gloves designed for a variety of uses in different seasons. For all of them, our key testing consideration was whether the gloves were truly waterproof. To find out, we used three testing methods and allowed the gloves to thoroughly dry between tests. All comments about sizing are subjective, based on sizing guides provided by the manufacturers and perceived comfort by the tester. On those gloves not listed as unisex, women tested women’s gloves, and men tested men’s gloves.

Industry observers note that first, we simulated storm conditions with a rain-wand attachment on a garden hose. The testers wore each pair of gloves beneath a steady 2-minute shower, flexing their hands and turning them over to expose all parts of the gloves to the stream. In the second test, we immersed our gloved hands into a bucket of water, again flexing and rotating to ensure that they were completely wet. Finally, we tested them for wet-gripping ability while handling smooth wet stones. To merit inclusion in this guide, each pair of gloves passed all three tests with minimal water intrusion to the inside of the glove.

Before shopping for the best waterproof gloves, consider the type of work planned for the gloves as well as the kind of materials and construction desired. In this section, we review some key considerations to keep in mind while shopping for the best waterproof gloves, including materials, use, fit, and more.

Choosing the best waterproof gloves depends on how they’ll be used. Work gloves are completely different from those intended for outdoor sports or casual wear.

In a recent development, on garments labeled “waterproof,” the outer shell is usually where the magic happens. Materials like tightly woven nylon, polyester, softshell technical materials, treated leather, and others work well to shed water before it can seep through to the lining. Keep in mind that it’s very rare for leather gloves to actually be waterproof; more likely, they are simply water-resistant.

Aside from shell material, other elements in waterproof gloves’ exteriors make them useful in wet or messy situations. Some of the best waterproof gloves, for example, have textured grips that make it easier for the wearer to grab on to wet, slippery surfaces, making them ideal for skiing, cycling, and other active pursuits. Those looking for waterproof gloves for work may want to invest in gloves with reinforced palms and thumbs, which should last longer and stand up to more wear.

The best waterproof gloves contain an optional outer shell with conductors that transfer the electrical charge from a finger to a touch screen, allowing customers to manipulate their phones without removing their gloves.

Industry observers note that some of the best waterproof gloves contain insulation that captures body heat, which forms air pockets that warm with the heat from the hand. Most insulation is a man-made poly-fill material such as Thinsulate or 3M.

To ensure gloves keep warm air inside and cold air from seeping in, some waterproof gloves have long elastic cuffs that hug tight to the wrist and arm, closing off any pathway for air to enter. For even warmer gloves, look for removable liners that can slip inside a waterproof glove to add another layer of insulation.

When selecting the best waterproof gloves, fit and comfort are essential. However, a “good fit” is relative to the activity. A pair of running gloves fits quite differently than a pair of winter work gloves or ski gloves.

Waterproof running or hiking gloves often feel like a stretchy, flexible second skin. Because they’re lightweight and wick away moisture, consumers sometimes forget they’re even wearing them.

In a recent development, waterproof work gloves are bulkier and a bit stiff because they’re generally made from thick nylon or leather that resists ripping, tearing, and friction. Moreover, extra padding or reinforcement on the thumbs or palms can add to their bulk. Though work gloves fit loosely, they shouldn’t be so loose that it’s difficult to pick up small items while wearing them.

Ski gloves are flexible but don’t wear particularly well because they’re typically made from materials like nylon. Properly fitting ski gloves fit snugly around the wrist but are roomy enough to allow the skier to manipulate straps on ski poles and boot bindings.

Also consider breathability. If hands sweat and moisture collects inside the glove, it won’t matter that the shell is waterproof because hands will still get wet. Breathable gloves help some of the heat and moisture escape without letting in cold outer air and moisture.

Now that you know a bit more about the factors to consider when choosing the best waterproof gloves for your needs, some questions may remain. The following are some of the most frequently asked questions about the best waterproof gloves, so check for an answer to your question below.

Waterproof means that absolutely no water makes its way into the glove. Water-resistant means that the gloves shed water to a degree before water comes in.

As one of the best options for the warmest waterproof gloves, the Carhartt Cold Snap waterproof gloves are warm enough to protect your hands in very cold temperatures.

You can wash some waterproof gloves, but it’s best to spot clean them and use a boot dryer with a glove attachment if they become soiled.

The best way to dry the inside of waterproof gloves is to put them on a boot dryer with a glove attachment.
