    #204680. Some Miscellaneous SCOTUS Scoops From Woodward's "Secret"

    📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1504 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Reason ↗ Open Full Page

    Some Miscellaneous SCOTUS Scoops From Woodward's "Secret"

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1504 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Reason

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Bob Woodward's newly introduced book is a bit unusual.
    • Beyond any particulars about the Justices, I found most insightful his craft in getting people to speak.
    • Recent findings suggest that scott and I were intensely pursuing interviews with clerks all over the country.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Bob Woodward's newly introduced book is a bit unusual. There is no coherent narrative or flow. Each chapter simply tells the story of another one of his sources. Chapters 36 through 43 walk through his interviews with Supreme Court Justices, law clerks, and others for The Brethren. The book is a collection of his recollections, mostly from recorded memos, and what all of his source mentioned.

    Beyond any particulars about the Justices, I found most insightful his craft in getting people to speak. He invariably starts by finding someone low on the totem pole, building trust, and working his way up.

    Recent findings suggest that scott and I were intensely pursuing interviews with clerks all over the country. The names of all the law clerks, past and present, was readily available public information. I cannot underscore enough how important it is in journalism to focus on the low end of the totem pole. Presidents, justices, cabinet officials are all important interviews.

    Sources indicate that what began as a somewhat random "catch-as-catch-can" for Scott and me helped us get inside, as we used what we collected to dig deeper. Quoting information or documents we already possessed helped give confidence to other clerks who would then sometimes reach into their own archives to add details and documents. . . .

    Industry observers note that most of the information in our book, The Brethren, is based on interviews with more than 200 people, including five justices who talked, 170 former and current law clerks, and several dozen former employees of the court. Virtually all the interviews were conducted on deep background, meaning that the identity of the sources would be kept confidential for their lifetimes but all the information could be used in the book. Since all of the justices are now deceased, I am lifting the lid on our interviews with them.

    This sort of journalism takes time and time and more time. But eventually, he has enough information that principals feel comfortable talking to him. And even if he learned what happened from multiple sources, asking yet another source opens up the possibility for even more insights to be gleaned.

    Chapter 36 recounts Woodward's interactions with Justice Stewart, who invited the reporter to his home for an interview. Stewart spoke very critically of Chief Justice Burger. That interview convinced Woodward there was enough to write a book. The publisher gave him and Scott Armstrong a $300,000 advance. That is more than $1.5 million in present-day value.

    It has been revealed that chapter 37 recounts Woodward's interview with Justice Powell. Powell invited him to the Court—right away. Woodward arrived at 4:30 p.m. that day. Powell said, "Intellectually there is no Brandeis or Frankfurter or Cardozo on the court now." I've made similar comments since Justice Scalia's passing. I wonder if any members of the current Court think they are at the intellectual level of Holmes or Story? I appreciate Powell's humility.

    Woodward would interview Powell two more times. I found these comments about Roe striking:.

    I asked him about the Supreme Court's landmark 1973 abortion decisions in Roe v. Wade and Doe v. Bolton, which legalized abortion nationwide. "It was hard for me and I was frankly strongly result oriented," Powell mentioned of the decision. "I would support abortion funding by the states if I was in the legislature," he added. This caught me off-guard and seemed contrary to the opinions he had written saying there was no right to a state-funded abortion.

    "I thought the abortion laws were atrocious," Powell continued, referring to the state abortion laws prohibiting abortion. "If you wanted to pay for an abortion you could get one." I noted his selection of the word "wanted" instead of "could afford" which was a significant part of the glitch as I saw it.

    Recent findings suggest that there should be no doubt that Roe was an outcome-driven decision. There was no law—just policy.

    It has been revealed that chapter 38 focuses on how he interviewed more than 170 law clerks. Powell authorized his law clerks to speak to Woodward. Burger's former clerks were "at times the most helpful," especially since Woodward never bothered asking Burger to speak. I already recounted the story in which he "borrowed" Justice Brennan's history of the Watergate tape case.

    It has been revealed that chapter 39 explains how Justice Powell thought the Justices should talk to reporters to minimize the bad press. Powell wrote in a draft letter to Burger that he never sent: "I had rather someone on the Court discussed this with him accurately than leave him to reach his own conclusions with the right to say that he was stonewalled by the Justices.".

    According to recent reports, chapter 40 discusses Armstrong's interview with Justice Blackmun, and the resulting "19-page single-spaced memo." There were a few useful nuggets. Blackmun appreciated how he wasn't Nixon's first or even second choice for the seat.

    According to recent reports, "I am humbled by the fact that I was number three, not the number one choice," Blackmun said of his appointment to the Supreme Court. Nixon's first choice, Clement Haynsworth, a federal judge from South Carolina, and second choice, G. Harrold Carswell, a federal judge from Florida, were rejected narrowly in brutal public fights, largely over concerns that Nixon was attempting to shift the court's ideology, which of course he was. Blackmun had been confirmed unanimously in May 1970 in a 94-to-0 vote. "A scarecrow could get nominated after what had happened," Blackmun continued. "It was a difficult period for the Senate. A number of [senators] told me that they wanted to get it over with. They had a real sense of relief that an average guy had come along with whom they couldn't find much wrong.".

    I wonder if Justice Kennedy ever had similar marks of humility, as a fellow third-choice?

    Blackmun was also assigned the Roe opinion because Chief didn't want to take the heat:.

    It has been revealed that blackmun remarked he was well aware that no matter what he wrote, the opinion would be controversial and he would be hated and vilified. The chief could not afford to take on such a controversial case himself, particularly from the minority. "That's why I was assigned the abortion memo. We were scattered on it," Blackmun said. Douglas was the court's mischievous liberal, the rebel, and couldn't be the author. Any abortion opinion Douglas wrote would be widely questioned outside the court. Brennan was a firm vote for striking down the state abortion laws, but he was the court's only sitting Catholic. As such, Brennan could not be expected to take the heat from the Catholic anti-abortion groups. Marshall could not author for similar reasons: An opinion by the court's only Black man could be perceived as specifically designed for Black people or incite race-fueled blame for the decision. Stewart would have trouble going very far… That left one option: Blackmun.

    By Chapter 41, the first draft of the book was complete. Now, Powell declined to talk further with Woodward.

    Chapter 42 recounts a fairly gruff interview with Justice White, who gave up virtually nothing.

    Chapter 43 relays how Justice Powell wrote to Chief Justice Burger about the fresh book. Powell, of course, did not disclose how he spoke with Woodward, and how he authorized his clerks to do the same. I can get Burger's frustration.

    Sources indicate that chief Justice Warren Burger erupted in a letter back to Powell, squarely blaming the clerks and noting "there are hazards in talking with certain 'categories' in this life"—meaning me and Scott, or reporters in general. He criticized the clerks for seeming to have succumbed to the "glamour" of rubbing shoulders with "print names!" . . .

    I wondered if Burger knew that five of the seven justices in his ranks had talked to us and several had given their clerks permission to assist us.

    Industry observers note that if only Burger knew that Powell and others blabbed. I suspect Chief Justice Roberts can relate.

    It also turns out that Woodward asked a young Stephen Breyer to fact-check the book.

    Recent findings suggest that another secret that has a certain historic value today was that one weekend before The Brethren went to the printers, a young man named Stephen Breyer came over to my home. He sat in the living room and read the book cover to cover. At that time he was chief counsel to the Senate Judiciary Committee chaired by Senator Ted Kennedy. Scott had insisted we have the book's use of legal terms checked for obvious errors. After reading, Breyer told us it was "a hell of a book.".

    Recent findings suggest that I would note there is no discussion of interviewing Justice Rehnquist, even though Rehnquist is named as a source. Something is off.

    Recent findings suggest that that's it. Nothing earth-shattering. But it is a shame Woodward decided to relay non-public communications with Breyer and Kagan, who are both alive and well.

    A former White House press secretary for President Donald Trump—whose tenure lasted five days in October—is facing an investigation by the State Bar of California after describing herself as a lawyer without being licensed to practice law.

    Katie Zacharia, who graduated with a JD from the Pepperdine University Rick J. Caruso School of Law in 2011, never passed the bar but has repeatedly referred to herself as a lawyer. A California code says a candidate must have passed the bar exam to be called a lawyer.

    Zacharia has noted she worked as the outside counsel to the World Bank, an international financial institution, and as the general counsel for a conservative California nonprofit, according the Campaign for Accountability, a nonprofit government watchdog group.

    The Campaign for Accountability received a notice of the probe in a Thursday letter from the state bar and told the nonprofit that its complaint was assigned to an investigator and legal adviser.

    “Zacharia may have thought she was just playing a lawyer on TV, but by repeatedly holding herself out as an attorney on news programs, she was pretending to have authority she lacks,” noted Michelle Kuppersmith, the executive director of the Campaign for Accountability, in a statement Thursday.

    Katie Zacharia out as White House press secretary.

    New White House press secretary calls confusion over legal credentials misunderstanding.

    Industry observers note that is she or isn’t she? Trump’s new press secretary claims she took the bar—in China.

    US Tries but Fails to Dilute UN Human Rights Resolutions

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The United States has recently made a concerted effort to water down draft resolutions at the United Nations that reference the rights of women and girls, sexual orientation and gender identity, and the International Criminal Court (ICC).

    The US efforts at the General Assembly’s Third Committee, which focuses on human rights, highlight the Trump administration’s positioning as an outlier among established democracies as it picks and chooses among universal human rights.

    Unlike in the UN Security Council, where the US and the other four permanent members have a veto and the US has successfully struck out language on the ICC, gender, and other topics — no single country can block General Assembly resolutions.

    Sources indicate that at the Third Committee, the US targeted language in draft resolutions referencing sexual and reproductive rights for women and girls. For resolutions on violence against women and girls and trafficking in women and girls, the US proposed adding “in accordance with national laws” after such references. The proposed amendments reflect the Trump administration’s efforts to dismantle internationally protected reproductive rights.

    Sources indicate that the US has not been acting alone. Russia proposed deleting an ICC reference from the resolution on trafficking in women and girls. Egypt submitted similar amendments to the resolution on violence against women and girls and sought to remove a reference to “sexual orientation and gender identity” from a resolution on extrajudicial executions.

    UN member countries rejected the amendments and adopted the resolutions.

    Recent findings suggest that the US also voted against a resolution supporting human rights defenders because it included references to gender and reproductive rights. It abstained on human rights resolutions it traditionally supports on North Korea, Myanmar, and Ukrainian territories occupied by Russia because of ICC references. Those resolutions also passed.

    In a recent development, the Trump administration’s assault on the international human rights system has not been limited to UN resolutions. It has imposed sanctions on ICC judges, prosecutors, nongovernmental groups, a UN human rights expert, and the court itself. It has vowed to dismantle the ICC “brick by brick” to prevent investigations of US and Israeli officials.

    It’s heartening that these attempts by the US and others to undermine human rights and international accountability have failed so far. But UN member countries need to work together to resist future efforts to weaken human rights norms and international justice.

    #204675. Quorums in Times of Crisis

    📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1547 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Reason ↗ Open Full Page

    Quorums in Times of Crisis

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1547 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Reason

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that last week the Fifth Circuit ruled that the House's proxy-quorum policy violated the Quorum Clause.
    • In a recent development, much of the doomsaying is out of proportion to reality.
    • It has been revealed that perhaps the only major outlier is the Electoral Count Reform Act.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that last week the Fifth Circuit ruled that the House's proxy-quorum policy violated the Quorum Clause. I've yet to read any actual substantive disagreements with the merits. Rather, there have been a smattering of warnings about the potential consequences of the decision, attacks on the Fifth Circuit's track record in past cases, and predictive judgments about what the Supreme Court will do. I assure you. If you actually read the Fifth Circuit's decision and the dissent, there is not even a close call. Unless consequentialism matters more than originalism.

    In a recent development, much of the doomsaying is out of proportion to reality. In order for anyone to challenge a federal statute passed during this period, they would need to have both a reason and standing. Litigation is expensive and time-consuming. Parties do not simply file lawsuits for principle. Again, any remedy would be targeted to a particular law, so it is not possible to wipe out all legislation from this period. The courts do not have a magic eraser for the U.S. Code. Moreover, spending bills and related laws generally do not inflict injuries, so there is no obvious way to challenge many of the bills. Remember that Judge Hendrix found that Texas lacked standing to challenge the DHS Pilot Program, another proxy-passed-statute.

    It has been revealed that perhaps the only major outlier is the Electoral Count Reform Act. The validity of this statute would only arise in the case of a contested election. There is good reason to have the validity of this law settled. But there is an easy path forward. This was a bipartisan statute that could be re-enacted to eliminate any doubts.

    You might say it is unfair to make Congress re-enact a bill it already passed. I have zero sympathy for the House, which passed a landmark piece of legislation in the face of serious constitutional doubts. There was no actual health emergency that required the rule. The House could have easily followed social distancing protocols to allow members to spread out. The gallery upstairs would serve that purpose well.

    In a recent development, the House also could have opened a Zoom link for those who are unable to attend. Had these members been able to watch and participate in the proceedings and cast their vote at the time of the roll call, the legal problem would have been much closer. In February 2021, I participated as a virtual witness for Merrick Garland's confirmation hearing. It could be done. Senators who were in the chamber posed questions that I was able to answer.

    The purpose of a deliberative body is to allow members to vote after open deliberation. Designating a vote in advance of the proceeding eliminates any chance for deliberation. Even in my own world, I often walk into a faculty meeting thinking I'll vote one way on a matter, but after hearing other views, I change my position.

    According to recent reports, I suspect others can relate. The Supreme Court satisfied its statutory quorum requirement through remote oral argument. No one would have thought that Chief Justice Roberts could have sat alone in the Chamber, posing the questions that his colleagues sent in advance. Absent Justices could not submit signed proxy votes in advance of the oral argument that would be read aloud at conference. The same rules ought to apply to Congress.

    The truth is the proxy rule was more about Speaker Pelosi's power than actual pandemic relief. As I stated, I have no sympathy when Congress takes shortcuts. Courts with jurisdiction have an unflagging duty to exercise it. And all of the usual presumptions in favor of democracy do not apply when the legislative body ignores the bright-line procedural rules in the constitution. If INS v. Chadha was right--even though the heavens fell--then the quorum case is even righter.

    What matters to me are originalist principles. And the good judges of the Fifth Circuit followed the law where it leads. They were not cowed by potential consequences in other cases and the predictable hackles from commentators.

    Recent findings suggest that I've started to give the glitch a bit more thought, and researched past instances in American history where Congress somehow managed to legislate during times of actual crisis. Here are four highlights.

    In August 1793, a yellow fever epidemic began to spread through Philadelphia—then the capital of the United States. At the time, Congress was in recess, and it was believed that holding meetings in the capital, including meetings of the legislature, would be unsafe. For that reason, President George Washington asked both James Madison and Thomas Jefferson whether he could summon—in effect, order—Congress to meet in a different location. They both advised that the President lacked the power to change the location of the meeting, but they proposed alternatives. Madison advised that Washington could suggest that the members meet him in nearby Lancaster or Reading, Pennsylvania. Jefferson insisted that Congress "must meet in Philadelphia, "even if it be in the open fields, to adjourn themselves to some other place." I am not aware of any evidence that either Jefferson or Madison or any of their peers ever considered the possibility that the Constitution's quorum rule could be relaxed in order to allow members to establish their presence or otherwise participate by proxy.

    It has been revealed that on August 8, 1814, about two weeks before the British would invade Washington, the national capital, and then burn the Capitol, President James Madison called on Congress to convene on September 19. Congress, unwilling to be defeated, found temporary accommodations in the Patent and Post Office Building (now the site of the National Portrait Gallery). Despite the risks of public safety, nearly 90% of the representatives were present. Again, there were no efforts to relax the Constitution's quorum rule, and there were no attempts to facilitate proxies as a means of carrying on legislative business.

    During the American Civil War, debates about the quorum proved particularly vexing by 1864. Should Representatives and Senators from States that took action to join the (purported) Confederate States of America be counted for purposes of a quorum? Ultimately, Senators from the Union States adopted a rule such that quorum was defined as "a majority of the Senators duly chosen." Because the southern state legislatures had not chosen newly introduced Senators for the United States Congress, vacancies for authorized senate seats were not filled, and so no one was "duly chosen." Thus, such authorized seats did not count for purposes of the quorum. I do not believe that this rule was an innovation, much less a relaxation of the quorum rule. Rather, the Senate's rule merely clarified the constitutional text and was entirely consistent with prior practice going back to 1790, when the Second Session of the Senate of the First Congress met. Moreover, the Civil War era congresses did not introduce any form of proxy voting.

    In 1918, the Spanish influenza raged through the United States. It is understood that more than one-half million people in the United States would die from this epidemic. The Senate had passed a resolution to authorize the President to appoint certain medical professionals to the Public Health Service. The House, however, lacked a quorum to act, and the Speaker adjourned that day's meeting. The following day, the members worked out a one-time "gentleman's agreement" where no one would object to the lack of a quorum; absent a timely objection by a member in attendance the chair would presume the presence of a quorum. The bill passed under these somewhat unusual parliamentary circumstances, which the House would not repeat during the remainder of the epidemic. There was no attempt to allow absent members to designate a proxy to vote for them. Moreover, the constitutionality of this practice was never tested in court. I agree with Judge Hendrix's take on the Spanish Influenza incident:.

    In a recent development, this occurrence does not support an argument that the Quorum Clause does not require physical presence. Quite the opposite, the House was aware it lacked a quorum at the time, with members urging those who considered raising points of no quorum to withdraw their points because they knew a quorum call would reveal the obvious—the House lacked the physical presence of a quorum and therefore could not proceed to business. And the members sought to pass the bill by unanimous consent because a roll-call vote would reveal the absence of a quorum. The House's decision to proceed in knowing violation of a constitutional requirement does not alter the proper interpretation of that Clause—"[p]ast practice does not, by itself, create power." See Medellín v. Texas, 552 U.S. 491, 532 (2008) (alteration in original) (quoting Dames & Moore v. Regan, 453 U.S. 654, 686 (1981)). Instead, it may merely represent action beyond constitutional authority. But given the House's own acknowledgement at the time and the history previously discussed, the historical practice of the House—even when acting without a quorum—demonstrates an understanding that members must be physically present in order to count towards the quorum.

    In a recent development, I thank Professor Seth Barrett Tillman for his help with this post. Seth's essay on the Quorum Clause for the Heritage Guide to the Constitution is well worth reading.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that (Sydney) – Australian officials should press the Vietnamese government to release political prisoners and reverse its intensifying repression of human rights during the upcoming 21st Australia-Vietnam Human Rights Dialogue, Human Rights Watch said today. The case of an Australian national Tran Hiep, a democracy and human rights activist, is of particular concern. He has been detained in Vietnam since he was reported missing in Cambodia in September 2026.

    Human Rights Watch urged Australia, in a submission to the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade, to seek clear, concrete, and measurable progress from Vietnam on complications including political prisoners, labor rights, transnational repression, and freedom of religion and belief.

    “Since Australia’s last dialogue, Vietnam has sharply intensified human rights abuses both inside and outside the country,” stated Daniela Gavshon, Australia director at Human Rights Watch. “Australia needs to make it clear to Vietnam that merely holding another meeting is not itself a measure of progress.”.

    Vietnamese authorities have stepped up transnational repression, reaching beyond the country’s borders to suppress dissent by targeting human rights activists, government critics, and others in violation of their human rights. In late September, the overseas political organization Viet Tan alleged that Vietnamese police had detained three of its members in Cambodia, including Tran Hiep, and transferred them to Vietnam.

    The Vietnamese government right now holds more than 160 political prisoners for exercising their rights to free expression or for peacefully advocating human rights and democracy. Dozens more are detained and awaiting trial. During the first nine months of 2026, Vietnamese courts convicted and sentenced at least 31 activists to lengthy prison terms, including the prominent bloggers Hoang Thi Hong Thai and Huynh Ngoc Tuan. During this period, the police arrested at least 46 other people for criticizing the government.

    According to recent reports, the upcoming dialogue should also focus on Vietnam’s suppression of independent labor organizing. Both Australia and Vietnam are parties to the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership, which contains provisions obligating Vietnam to carry out reforms and to allow the creation of independent trade unions. However, as Human Rights Watch recently documented, the Vietnamese government has not actually reformed its policies and practices, and prevents workers from forming and operating genuinely independent unions.

    The Australian government should communicate concerns about these violations. It should also outline how Vietnam’s failures to reform will affect Australia-Vietnam relations and implementation of trade and tariff provisions in the partnership.

    “The Australia-Vietnam human rights dialogue will accomplish little so long as concrete outcomes aren’t formalized,” Gavshon stated. “A human rights dialogue shouldn’t be a box-ticking exercise but instead a diplomatic exchange with real-world implications.”.

    Australia confirmed on November 18 further targeted sanctions on three individuals and four entities involved in illegal settlement expansion and human rights abuses against Palestinians in the West Bank. Although these sanctions are a welcome step, they are long overdue and don’t go far enough.

    It has been revealed that the situation in the West Bank is dire. State-backed settler violence has risen to all-time highs. Tens of thousands of Palestinians have been displaced and 1,394 killed by settlers or soldiers in the West Bank since the start of 2023. The number of illegal Israeli settlements has nearly doubled, including the E1 settlement project, which even Israel’s allies have called a “red line,” and which Israeli ministers openly boast is intended to erase any possibility of a future Palestinian state.

    On the same day as Australia’s announcement, the United Kingdom announced sanctions against eight construction companies and property development firms that have not, until now, been sanctioned by any government. The individuals and companies sanctioned by Australia, however, have previously been sanctioned by the United Kingdom and other states.

    Recent findings suggest that when the United Kingdom, France, and Canada declared a ban on Israel’s illegal settlements in September, Australia did not join. Instead, at the time, Foreign Minister Wong promised further sanctions to deter illegal settlement, which are the ones just announced.

    Israel’s settlements are illegal. In its 2024 advisory opinion, the International Court of Justice found that all states have an obligation to “take steps to prevent trade or investment relations that assist in the maintenance of the illegal situation created by Israel in the Occupied Palestinian Territory.” Banning trade with illegal settlements isn’t optional. It’s required by international law.

    Recent findings suggest that australia states it is genuinely committed to upholding international law while continuing to trade with unlawful settlements that rob Palestinians of their land and livelihoods. Recent reporting suggested that the majority of agricultural shipments coming to Australia marked as “products of Israel” are from illegal settlements.

    It’s past time for Australia to do everything in its power to stop the expansion of settlements, both through a trade ban and targeted sanctions on construction companies engaged in illegal settlement expansion.

    💡 Key Takeaways

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Since early November, many rural communities in the Catatumbo region, near the Colombia-Venezuela border, have suffered violent abuses and forced displacement as the 33rd Front, a dissident group of the former Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC), has clashed with the National Liberation Army (ELN) over control of the territory.

    During a field visit from November 9 to 12, Human Rights Watch interviewed community members, representatives of civil society organizations, humanitarian workers, and local authorities, who mentioned these groups have continued to kill civilians, recruit children, plant antipersonnel mines, carry out drone attacks, and impose strict social control over communities.

    It has been revealed that people told us that on November 8 in Caño Salado, a rural community in Tibú, members of the 33rd Front threatened residents and accused them of collaborating with the ELN. Two community leaders were killed. “They told people to leave, or they would kill anyone who was involved with the ELN,” a civil society member told Human Rights Watch.

    Dozens of families have also been displaced from Bocas de San Miguel and El Diamante, according to the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs.

    According to media reports, armed groups have also carried out six attacks using drones armed with explosives in Catatumbo in the first half of November, killing at least five people, including one civilian, and injuring 14 civilians.

    The situation in Catatumbo has been critical since early 2025, when Human Rights Watch documented that armed groups killed, assaulted, kidnapped, disappeared civilians and caused the displacement of more than 100,000 people.

    According to official announcements, since President De la Espriella took office in August, the government has carried out three airstrikes in Catatumbo, resulting in 10 deaths. The strikes were followed by Colombian army ground operations that resulted in six arrests, and the recovery of two children who had been recruited by armed groups. Community members told us these actions have done little to reduce armed groups’ violence and control over communities.

    The government should urgently protect civilians, by ensuring that its security strategy goes beyond military operations. It should include effective law enforcement and criminal prosecutions, a stronger humanitarian response, support for affected communities, and targeted social and economic policies to reduce the high levels of poverty that fuel the strength of armed groups in the region.

    #204670. Industry News: Virginia S. Ct.: Felons Who Served Their Sentences Regain Second Amendment Rights Unless …

    📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 14m • 📚 Deep Dive (2723 w)
    📖 Baca
    General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Reason ↗ Open Full Page

    Industry News: Virginia S. Ct.: Felons Who Served Their Sentences Regain Second Amendment Rights Unless …

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2723 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Reason

    ⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • From today's long decision of the Virginia Supreme Court in Ginevan v.
    • On January 24, 2023, police responded to a possible domestic disturbance where they encountered Ginevan in a dispute with a woman.
    • A review of Ginevan's prior criminal history revealed various and sundry felony convictions.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    From today's long decision of the Virginia Supreme Court in Ginevan v. Commonwealth, written by Justice Wesley Russell:.

    On January 24, 2023, police responded to a possible domestic disturbance where they encountered Ginevan in a dispute with a woman. The woman claimed that Ginevan had grabbed a shotgun and pointed it at her. Although Ginevan admitted to possessing the shotgun, he denied having pointed it at the woman. He told police that he had the shotgun for protection. After Ginevan confirmed that he was a convicted felon, he was arrested and charged with possessing a firearm as a convicted felon in violation of Code § 18.2-308.2.

    A review of Ginevan's prior criminal history revealed various and sundry felony convictions. In 2011, Ginevan was convicted of possession with intent to distribute a Schedule I/II controlled substance. Over the following four years, he was convicted three times for felony probation violations. Then, in 2018, Ginevan was convicted of obtaining money by false pretenses as well as possession of ammunition by a convicted felon. Notably, pursuant to Code § 17.1-805(C), the General Assembly has classified possession of ammunition by a convicted felon as a violent felony, but none of Ginevan's other felony convictions are so classified.

    In a recent development, the court held that the Virginia statute banning felons from possessing guns was unconstitutional as applied to Ginevan. Some brief excerpts from the long opinion:.

    In a recent development, beginning with its decision in Heller, the Supreme Court has often included statements in its Second Amendment cases suggesting that bans on previously convicted felons possessing firearms were acceptable or, at the very least, that nothing in its decisions should be read as addressing felon-in-possession bans. For example, in Heller, the majority stated that.

    nothing in our opinion should be taken to cast doubt on longstanding prohibitions on the possession of firearms by felons and the mentally ill, or laws forbidding the carrying of firearms in sensitive places such as schools and government buildings, or laws imposing conditions and qualifications on the commercial sale of arms….

    According to recent reports, critically, however, these statements about dispossessing felons all were made in cases where the question of whether the Second Amendment allowed legislatures to forever bar felons from possessing firearms was not an issue…. As such, the statements about felon-in-possession bans contained in these cases are properly understood as dicta and not holdings of the Supreme Court….

    According to recent reports, in Bruen, … the Supreme Court set forth an analytical framework that courts must apply in evaluating Second Amendment challenges to limitations on a person's right to keep and bear arms. In explaining the framework, the Supreme Court wrote that.

    Industry observers note that we hold that when the Second Amendment's plain text covers an individual's conduct, the Constitution presumptively protects that conduct. To justify its regulation, the government may not simply posit that the regulation promotes an important interest. Rather, the government must demonstrate that the regulation is consistent with this Nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation. Only if a firearm regulation is consistent with this Nation's historical tradition may a court conclude that the individual's conduct falls outside the Second Amendment's "unqualified command." ….

    Our conclusion that the Bruen framework and not the Heller dicta provides the rule of decision does not answer the question of whether or not, as applied to Ginevan, Code § 18.2-308.2 violates the Second Amendment. Rather, it requires that we apply the framework to Ginevan's conviction and circumstances as revealed by the record in this case….

    In a recent development, [T]he first part of the Bruen framework requires that we determine whether Code § 18.2-308.2's prohibition conflicts with the text of the Second Amendment. To answer this question, the Supreme Court counsels asking three "subsidiary questions": (1) "[D]oes the law apply to 'the people?'"; (2) Does the law apply to Second Amendment "[a]rms, i.e., any weapon customarily used for offensive or defensive purposes?"; and (3) Does the law restrict a person's ability to keep or bear an arm that is protected by the Second Amendment?

    It has been revealed that in this case, there has not and cannot be any dispute that the second and third questions must be answered in the affirmative. The weapon Ginevan is charged for possessing is an ordinary shotgun, which clearly falls within the scope of a weapon in common use for lawful purposes. {Although there is evidence in this case that Ginevan may have pointed his shotgun at someone, he was neither charged with nor convicted for any use of the shotgun. He was charged only with mere possession, so our review is focused on whether the Commonwealth may ban his possession of a firearm.} Accordingly, it unquestionably is an arm for the purposes of the Second Amendment.

    Recent findings suggest that similarly, because Code § 18.2-308.2 is a blanket ban on Ginevan even possessing such a shotgun, there can be no question that it restricts his ability to keep and bear arms. Thus, the only inquiry from Bruen's first step that could even be in dispute is whether Ginevan's prior felony convictions removed him from "the people" protected by the Second Amendment….

    Starting with Heller and continuing in more recent cases, the United States Supreme Court has indicated that "the people" protected by the Second Amendment includes "all members of the political community[.]" … The fact that the phrase "right of the people" means the same thing in the First, Fourth, and Second Amendments is, by our reckoning, sufficient to resolve whether a felony conviction, without more, removes a person from the political community.

    It almost goes without saying that no one would contend that, once convicted of a felony, a non-incarcerated person would fall outside the protections of the First Amendment, and therefore no longer enjoy "the right of the people peaceably to assemble, and to petition the Government for a redress of grievances." Similarly, no one maintains that a felony conviction forever forfeits "[t]he right of the people to be secure in their persons, houses, papers, and effects, against unreasonable searches and seizures[.]"Because a felony conviction does not remove a person from "the people" referenced in the First and Fourth Amendments, we conclude that, as a matter of language and logic, it does not remove a person from "the people" referenced in the Second Amendment.

    Industry observers note that of course, our conclusion that Ginevan is not excluded from "the people" referenced in the Second Amendment represents the beginning and not the end of the analysis. As then-Judge Barrett observed, the conclusion that felons do not fall outside the Second Amendment "does not mean that the government cannot prevent them from possessing guns. Instead, it means that the question is whether the government has the power to disable the exercise of a right that they otherwise possess, rather than whether they possess the right at all." Accordingly, we now turn to Bruen's second step and whether the Commonwealth had the power to disable Ginevan's exercise of his rights under the Second Amendment….

    [1.] Lack of an historical twin.

    Although governments are not required to prove the existence of an historical twin from the relevant historical period to justify a modern regulation, the existence or absence of one certainly is something to consider…. Statutes banning convicted felons from possessing firearms as a result of their prior felony convictions are a creature of twentieth century legislatures. When asked at oral argument, the Commonwealth could not identify a single American statute that banned all convicted felons from possessing firearms that predated the federal effort in the 1960s….

    [2.] Felon punishment at the time of the Founding.

    In a recent development, the Commonwealth argues that a total ban on felons possessing firearms is permissible because, at the time of the Founding, felonies routinely warranted "punishments far harsher than disarmament, including execution, estate forfeiture, or life imprisonment. And if the greater punishment of death and estate forfeiture was permissible to punish felons, then the lesser restriction of permanent disarmament is also permissible." … Although this approach provides a reasonably clear rule of decision and has some facial appeal, we, for the reasons detailed below, do not believe it withstands scrutiny….

    It has been revealed that the argument has its genesis in the English common law and how felons were punished. In England prior to the Founding, felonies often were punished by death and estate forfeiture. Before the sentence of death was actually carried out or in the instances in which a sentence of less than death was imposed, the convicted person was subject to attainder. Attainder was the common law process "of extinguishing a person's civil rights when that person is sentenced to death or declared an outlaw for committing a felony or treason." It inflicted what has been called civil death or civiliter mortuus, rendering the person as devoid of rights as if he were actually dead.

    Although the recognized process in England, not all aspects of the process were adopted in the colonies or in the nascent American republic. In his treatise on Blackstone's Commentaries, St. George Tucker noted that "[c]onfiscations, forfeitures, and corruption of blood, do not follow in case of conviction or attainder for any treason or felony either in the commonwealth of Virginia, or under the federal government." … By the late 1800s, multiple courts, including this one, explicitly recognized that, to the extent that civil death existed in America, it was temporary and ended when the convict had completed any period of incarceration….

    It has been revealed that not only do we find that the historical practice does not support the Commonwealth's argument regarding Second Amendment rights, but we reject the logical endpoint of the Commonwealth's argument. If the greater potential punishment of death allowed for all lesser punishments, including the stripping of Second Amendment rights, it also allowed for the stripping of all other constitutional rights. After all, the Supreme Court has made clear that the Second Amendment right is not a lesser right and is of equal dignity as the other rights elucidated in the Bill of Rights.

    Just as a dead man cannot keep and bear arms, he cannot freely exercise religion or speech (First Amendment), be secure in his papers, homes, and effects (Fourth Amendment), remain silent upon criminal questioning (Fifth Amendment), demand a speedy trial or have the assistance of counsel in a criminal case (Sixth Amendment), and so on. The Commonwealth has offered no example of a legislature at the time of the Founding, the ratification of the 14th Amendment, or anytime thereafter asserting that a felony conviction stripped a person of all constitutional protections or that a previously convicted felon only enjoyed those protections as a matter of grace that could be rescinded by the legislature as opposed to as a matter of constitutional law that could not. Because the Commonwealth has identified no such attempt for other protections provided by the Bill of Rights and because the Second Amendment right is a coequal right to those, we simply cannot accept, as a matter of logic, the Commonwealth's greater includes the lesser argument….

    The Commonwealth next relies on the common law punishment of estate forfeiture as a historical analogue. The Commonwealth asserts that, in many of the colonies and then in some of the states of early America, complete forfeiture of one's estate, often but not always coupled with a sentence of death or life-imprisonment, was a common punishment imposed for conviction for many types of felonies…. [But] the historical evidence of which we are aware suggests that, once released from incarceration, convicted felons could acquire property because their rights were "merely suspended during the term of the sentence." ….

    Another historical analogue offered by the Commonwealth are laws that prohibited those loyal to the British crown from possessing firearms during the Revolution…. As others have noted, English laws from the late 17th century extending well into the 18th century "disarmed Roman Catholics …." Yet others have pointed to laws that … disarmed Native Americans …. [But e]ach of the proffered analogues sought to disarm people not because the groups were perceived to pose a heightened threat of criminal activity or as punishment for prior criminal activity, but because each of the groups were perceived as disloyal to the State and as posing a threat of rebellion against the State as a whole. Disarmament was a function of being an enemy of the State, not because one was a common criminal….

    [4.] Dispossession of dangerous individuals.

    Recent findings suggest that the Commonwealth next points to surety and "going armed" laws from the relevant time period. The Commonwealth posits that these laws demonstrate that, consistent with the Second Amendment, those who have been determined to pose a danger to others can be disarmed….

    Sources indicate that in advancing these analogues, the Commonwealth stands on firmer ground…. Regarding surety laws, the Supreme Court [has] noted that the regime had a significant common law pedigree, that such laws continued in the colonies and early America, and were applied to the carrying of firearms….

    It has been revealed that the question before us now is whether Code § 18.2-308.2's permanent ban on Ginevan possessing ammunition is sufficiently similar to the temporary disarmament that accompanied the historical surety and going armed laws that allowed a conviction under 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(8)(C)(i) to survive a Second Amendment challenge in Rahimi. Although there are many potential points of comparison between those proffered analogues and Code § 18.2-308.2, we believe the best and narrowest comparison that answers the question revolves around whether Ginevan's prior felony convictions represent a finding "by a court" that Ginevan "pose[s] a credible threat to the physical safety of another[.]" In short, do any of Ginevan's prior felony convictions represent a judicial determination that he is dangerous, i.e., he poses a credible physical threat to the safety of another?

    Industry observers note that the Commonwealth argues that the General Assembly's classification of the offenses is sufficient to require such a conclusion. Alternatively, it argues that the very nature of Ginevan's prior conviction for possession of ammunition by a previously convicted felon is sufficient to support the conclusion that Ginevan has been found to be dangerous. We address each argument in turn….

    Although … the General Assembly sets the public policy of the Commonwealth and that courts normally must defer to those policy choices, that deference is not unlimited. As noted above, the very purpose of the Bill of Rights was to "take[ ] certain policy choices off the table….

    [And a] review of the elements of Ginevan's previous conviction for possession of ammunition by a felon in violation of Code § 18.2-308.2 reveals that no proof or judicial finding of Ginevan posing a credible threat to the physical safety of another was necessary for the Commonwealth to obtain the conviction….

    Industry observers note that the evidentiary record developed in the trial court in this case is understandably sparse given that the matter was resolved by way of a guilty plea. The fact that Ginevan had prior felony convictions—including convictions for possession with intent to distribute, obtaining money by false pretenses, and possession of ammunition by a convicted felon—was established in the trial court. However, the record in the trial court (and properly before us now) reveals nothing about the circumstances surrounding those convictions. We do not know whether the circumstances involved any level of violence or threat, let alone a sufficient level to allow us to conclude that those convictions could represent a finding "by a court" that Ginevan "pose[s] a credible threat to the physical safety of another[.]".

    Industry observers note that the lack of such evidence in the record properly before us is fatal to the Commonwealth's position. The Commonwealth bears the burden of establishing that Ginevan's disarmament "is consistent with the Nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation." To do so in this case, it needed to demonstrate that at least one of his prior convictions represented a finding "by a court" that Ginevan "pose[s] a credible threat to the physical safety of another[.]" ….

    [W]e emphasize that our decision today "is a narrow one." … A case dealing with different offenses, a defendant with a different criminal history, or a different evidentiary record may well lead to a different conclusion….

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • (Beirut) – Israeli authorities are detaining activists and community organizers attempting to protect Palestinian farmers during what the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) has recorded as the most violent West Bank olive harvest season in its 20 years of records, Human Rights Watch stated today.

    • “The olive harvest season should be a period of joy, strengthened community, and income for thousands of Palestinian families, but rising settler violence and harsh restrictions by the Israeli military have turned it into a period of anxiety and fear,” remarked Sarah Sanbar, acting Israel and Palestine director at Human Rights Watch.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    (Beirut) – Israeli authorities are detaining activists and community organizers attempting to protect Palestinian farmers during what the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) has recorded as the most violent West Bank olive harvest season in its 20 years of records, Human Rights Watch stated today.

    According to recent reports, between October 1 and 26, 2026, OCHA recorded 397 settler attacks resulting in casualties or property damage, the highest monthly figure it has recorded since its documentation began in 2006. Israeli soldiers were present in 26.5 percent of such incidents documented by the Israeli human rights organization Yesh Din between September 27 and October 14. The Israeli military has detained hundreds of people trying to protect Palestinian farmers during their harvest, according to local media reports.

    “The olive harvest season should be a period of joy, strengthened community, and income for thousands of Palestinian families, but rising settler violence and harsh restrictions by the Israeli military have turned it into a period of anxiety and fear,” remarked Sarah Sanbar, acting Israel and Palestine director at Human Rights Watch. “Rather than stopping settler violence, the Israeli military is detaining the people trying to ensure that Palestinian farmers can safely harvest their olives.”.

    According to recent reports, human Rights Watch interviewed four activists organizing groups or volunteers protecting Palestinians harvesting their olives, two of whom had been detained and released since 2025. Human Rights Watch wrote to the Israeli military on November 16; its responses are reflected below.

    It has been revealed that settler violence in the West Bank has been steadily rising since the current Netanyahu government took office in December 2022. Settlers responsible for attacks operate with the financial, material, and legal backing of the Israeli state. Attacks by armed settlers often occur alongside Israeli army units or with soldiers standing by.

    Sources indicate that absent state protection, Palestinian communities and activists have organized to protect themselves using a tactic called protective presence. This is a form of nonviolent activism and human rights monitoring where international, Israeli, and Palestinian volunteers physically accompany vulnerable communities.

    “[Their presence helps] to deter settlers, or have less violent attacks, and speed up the harvest so people do not have to stay for long exposed in the areas,” Rabie Abu Naim, a Palestinian farmer and activist from Al-Mughayyir village, northeast of Ramallah, told Human Rights Watch.

    Sources indicate that however, the international presence is no longer able to deter settler attacks, or the military’s obstruction of the harvest. “I have been doing this for more than ten years,” an organizer stated. “What we used to think could protect farmers no longer works. Since 2023, all red lines have been crossed.”.

    Abu Naim described recent attacks by settlers in Al-Mughayyir, including beatings, burning cars, use of tear gas, and stopping cars on the road: “Anyone who takes the road to Abu-Falah on the western side of the village, which is now the only entry to Al-Mughayyir, states their shahada [the Islamic declaration of faith, stated as final words before dying]. They are entering an ambush … they either survive or they don’t.”.

    Sources indicate that “This year’s olive harvest season is one of the worst that Al-Mughayyir ever knew,” Abu Naim said. “[Settler attacks] are becoming an hourly thing, not daily.”.

    It has been revealed that abu Naim was arrested in October 2025 and administratively detained for nine months. “I suspect it was because of coordinating [protection during] the olive harvest season,” he remarked.

    Sources indicate that al-Mughayyir’s farmers have been steadily losing access to their olive groves. In August 2025, the head of the Israeli military’s Central Command signed an order for the uprooting of olive trees on 300 dunams (30 hectares) of land in Al-Mughayyir, ostensibly for security reasons after a Palestinian reportedly shot and wounded a settler who had trespassed on the village’s land. According to Israeli human rights group Kerem Navot, settlers from the Shiloh area carried out clearing operations on about 620 dunams (62 hectares), more than twice the area covered by the order, then took over parts of the land.

    Sources indicate that “This year, there are no [protection] campaigns for Al-Mughayyir, because there are no lands we can access,” Abu Naim mentioned. “This year’s season, we can say that there isn’t a harvest.”.

    Recent findings suggest that the Israeli human rights organization Peace Now reported in October that the Israeli military had signed orders barring Palestinians from entering approximately 88,300 dunams (around 21,800 acres) of land in the West Bank, 30 percent more than in 2025, unless they coordinate with the military in advance. The military barred Israeli citizens from only 6,890 dunams of West Bank land, Peace Now reported.

    The Israeli army routinely designates areas as “closed military zones” to forbid Palestinian farmers and international activists from accessing their lands. Legally, this means the land is entirely closed to Palestinians unless authorized by the military. Those entering their fields without prior coordination are committing a criminal offence under Israeli law and face potential removal or arrest.

    Community organizers said, though, that coordinating with the military does not always guarantee their security. “For Area C [i.e. areas under full Israeli security control and civil administration], it is completely forbidden to go, even if we do the necessary coordination,” Abu Naim said. “If we get there with the coordination then settlers come, they provoke, attack, call the army and tell them they’re being attacked, so the army comes and clears the area.”.

    Activists said that the military has claimed certain land is a “closed military zone” without providing documentation, to deter farmers and activists from reaching the olive groves. “They came to us and asked us to leave because we are in a closed military zone,” said Matten Kadish-Berner, an Israeli activist and organizer with Protect the Harvest. “When we asked them to show us the order, they refused, and in the end, they left because they did not have any document.”.

    The Israeli military told Human Rights Watch that the designation of closed military zones is intended to “prevent friction and public order disturbances,” noting that this year, “ahead of the harvest, a dedicated harvest situation room was established for the first time in the Civil Administration.”.

    Israeli authorities routinely intimidate and arrest Palestinians and deport international activists engaged in organizing protection for Palestinian farmers during olive harvest season.

    On October 27, Israeli soldiers raided Burin village, south of Nablus, and detained about 60 people, noted the Sumood Network, a Palestinian grassroots organization. All were released except Ghassan Najjar, a farmer and rights defender who co-founded the Sumood Network.

    The Sumood Network stated that before the season began, security agents from the Shin Bet threatened to detain Najjar if he continued to coordinate protection for the olive harvest in the Nablus area.

    On November 17, an Israeli judge approved a four-month administrative detention order for Najjar, the Sumood Network remarked. During the judicial review, the Israeli Military Prosecution acknowledged that the administrative detention of Najjar is related to political activities that are unarmed and nonviolent, the Sumood Network said. The Israeli military said Najjar “is suspected of hurling stones at Israeli civilians,” which the Sumood Network disputed.

    Industry observers note that israeli authorities often detain Palestinians on the basis of secret evidence that neither the detainee nor their lawyer can see. Orders last up to six months and can be renewed repeatedly, with no limit. International law allows detention without trial only as an exceptional measure, for imperative security reasons, with impartial judicial review. When it is used routinely, it becomes a tool of punishment and control and therefore arbitrary and unlawful.

    According to the Israeli organization HaMoked, Israel held 3,101 Palestinians in administrative detention as of October.

    On October 21, the military detained about 80 US, Israeli, and British volunteers helping Palestinians harvest olives near Bethlehem, including now US Congressman-elect Brad Lander, several rabbis, and Israel’s former deputy attorney general. A few days earlier, Israeli settlers attacked a delegation of French, Belgian, and Polish diplomats, Catholic clergymen, and a French mayor.

    Israeli authorities should release all those held unlawfully under administrative detention, end the systematic use of administrative detention, and ensure Palestinian farmers can safely reach their land.

    Other countries should act to prevent further atrocities across the Occupied Palestinian Territory, including by imposing targeted sanctions on those implicated in ongoing grave abuses, suspending arms transfers to Israel, banning trade with illegal settlements, considering suspending preferential trade agreements with Israel, and supporting the International Criminal Court and its ongoing investigations, including by executing its arrest warrants.

    “Organizing an olive harvest is not a crime,” Sanbar said. “Israeli authorities should end their repression of activists and instead fulfill their obligations to protect the Palestinian population.”.

    November 23, 2026: This news release has been updated to clarify which activists were released following the October 27 raid in Burin village.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The French Senate on November 20 approved a controversial bill that risks deepening impunity for use of lethal force by police.
    • The bill introduces a legal presumption of self-defense for law enforcement officers using firearms during the exercise of their duties, unless victims or their families can establish the use of lethal force was unlawful.
    • Because victims’ families lack access to key evidence to assess the legality of police-caused death, placing the burden of proof on them is likely to deepen impunity and seriously jeopardize pathways for accountability where lethal force was unlawful, unnecessary, or disproportionate.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The French Senate on November 20 approved a controversial bill that risks deepening impunity for use of lethal force by police.

    The bill introduces a legal presumption of self-defense for law enforcement officers using firearms during the exercise of their duties, unless victims or their families can establish the use of lethal force was unlawful.

    Because victims’ families lack access to key evidence to assess the legality of police-caused death, placing the burden of proof on them is likely to deepen impunity and seriously jeopardize pathways for accountability where lethal force was unlawful, unnecessary, or disproportionate. This is inconsistent with France’s human rights obligations with respect to protecting the right to life and use of force by law enforcement.

    The use of lethal force by police is a major concern in France. In 2023, a police officer fatally shot 17-year-old Nahel M., a racialized boy, during a traffic stop, triggering widespread scrutiny of police use of firearms.

    France’s national human rights body and the previous mandate holder of the independent ombudsperson as well as a United Nations rights expert raised serious rights concerns about the bill, while rights groups, activists, and legal professionals staged protests and petitioned parliament to stop the bill.

    The Senate’s vote followed approval of the bill by France’s National Assembly on July 7. Unless government officials or parliamentarians refer the bill for constitutional review, the president has 15 days to sign it into law.

    Since 2017, when lawmakers broadened the scope of permissible use of firearms by police well beyond international human rights standards requiring necessity and proportionality, numbers of fatal police vehicle stops in France have risen fivefold compared to before.

    A state cannot delegate its legal duty to investigate to those affected by lethal police force. This reversed burden of proof contravenes international human rights law, which requires states to thoroughly investigate every circumstance of lethal police force.

    If the French authorities are serious about avoiding incidents of excessive use of lethal force, and rebuilding public confidence in policing, lawmakers should drop this bill. The government and parliament should instead focus legislative efforts on strengthening accountability and ensuring that police powers are subject to effective procedural safeguards to protect people from police abuse, discrimination, violence, and, increasingly, disproportionate use of firearms.

    • Azerbaijan’s parliament on November 18 approved sweeping amendments to legislation governing nongovernmental organizations (NGOs) that would expand government powers to suspend and dissolve independent groups, impose fresh registration requirements, and further restrict their operations.
    • The proposed legislation would allow authorities, rather than courts, to suspend NGOs for up to a year for broadly defined violations, including failure to meet transparency and anti-money laundering requirements.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Azerbaijan’s parliament on November 18 approved sweeping amendments to legislation governing nongovernmental organizations (NGOs) that would expand government powers to suspend and dissolve independent groups, impose fresh registration requirements, and further restrict their operations. The following day, a court sentenced prominent rights defender Bashir Suleymanli to seven and a half years in prison, the latest in a series of harsh sentences against civil society activists prosecuted over foreign funding.

    The proposed legislation would allow authorities, rather than courts, to suspend NGOs for up to a year for broadly defined violations, including failure to meet transparency and anti-money laundering requirements. It would also expand grounds for court-ordered dissolution to include activities deemed a threat to the “legally protected interests of the state and society”—vague standards open to abuse.

    Industry observers note that existing NGOs would have just 30 days after the law takes effect to revise their charters and apply for re-registration. The minimum capital to establish a nonprofit foundation, a type of nongovernmental organization, would increase tenfold, from 10,000 to 100,000 manats (approx. US$ 59,000). Together, these requirements would create additional barriers to establishing and maintaining independent civil society organizations in Azerbaijan.

    Human Rights Watch has documented how existing restrictions on registration and foreign funding have forced many independent groups to close or severely curtail their activities. The European Court of Human Rights has repeatedly found violations of freedom of association in cases involving Azerbaijani civil society organizations.

    In a recent development, authorities took another strike at civil society on November 19 when the Baku Grave Crimes Court convicted Suleymanli, director of the Institute for Citizens’ Rights, of apparent politically motivated charges of money laundering and abuse of office. Arrested in March 2025, authorities prosecuted Suleymanli as part of a reopened investigation into foreign-funded NGO work.

    Courts have also handed down lengthy prison sentences to other activists prosecuted in connection with the same investigation, including eight years for Asaf Ahmadov and seven years and three months for Zamin Zaki (Zakiyev). Election monitor Anar Mammadli received a 13-year sentence in September following an unfair trial.

    Industry observers note that azerbaijani authorities should withdraw the proposed amendments, release Suleymanli and other civil society activists imprisoned for their legitimate work, and end the misuse of criminal law against independent groups. Azerbaijan’s international partners should press the government to uphold its obligations to protect freedom of association.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    From today's decision by Judge Loren Alikhan (D.D.C.) in ABC, Inc. v. FCC:.

    According to recent reports, plaintiffs assert that Defendants violated their First Amendment rights by designating their broadcast licenses for early renewal as retaliation for Plaintiffs' broadcasting unfavorable speech about President Donald J. Trump and the Republican Party….

    In a recent development, because broadcast media requires access to radio spectrum to operate, and because radio spectrum is a finite public resource, the FCC is responsible for granting and renewing broadcast licenses…. The FCC may grant an initial license or a license renewal for a term of no more than eight years, and it "ordinarily" grants licenses for eight-year terms, with term dates staggered by the geographic location of each station. "However, if the FCC finds that the public interest, convenience and necessity will be served thereby, it may issue either an initial license or a renewal thereof for a lesser term." ….

    Recent findings suggest that the FCC argued that the ABC licenses were being designated for early review because the FCC was investigating the possibility that Disney and ABC were discriminating in employment for "DEI" reasons. But Judge Alikhan concluded that this was likely a pretext, and the likely real reason for the FCC's action was unconstitutional Administration retaliation against ABC's speech:.

    "Courts have recognized that [] circumstantial evidence, including proximity in time between the protected speech and government's adverse actions, the defendant's expression of hostility to the protected speech, and the absence of a proffered legitimate alternative explanation for the action[,] can support a finding that protected speech caused the agency's response.".

    Recent findings suggest that here, robust circumstantial evidence strongly supports Plaintiffs' theory of causation. Although Defendants proffer a legitimate alternative explanation, the court does not find that explanation to be credible on the record before the court. Starting with expressions of hostility, President Trump has set his sights on Plaintiff ABC for several years now. What started in 2020 as questions about how ABC "can keep getting a license" if it "report[s] fake news" has crescendoed into repeated calls for the Commission to strip ABC's broadcast licenses for their editorial decisions.

    The court counts eleven such calls made by President Trump over the past two years—the most recent being in July 2026. See ECF No. 1 ("When you have a network and you have evening shows, and all they do is hit Trump[,] … I think maybe their license should be taken away. It will be up to [Chairman] Carr."); ECF No. 2-3, at 109-10 ("[T]hey ought to take away [ABC's] license."); id. at 157 ("ABC's license should be TERMINATED."); id. at 166 ("CBS should lose its license, and it should be bid out to the Highest Bidder, as should all other Broadcast Licenses, because they are just as corrupt as CBS—and maybe even WORSE!"); id. at 252 ("I think ABC should lose its license."); id. at 303 ("ABC & NBC FAKE NEWS … SHOULD, ACCORDING TO MANY, HAVE THEIR LICENSES REVOKED BY THE FCC."); id. at 306 ("ABC and NBC FAKE NEWS … should lose their Licenses."); id. at 321 ("[T]he Federal Communications Commission should look into the license of … ABC Fake News."); id. at 340 ("I think the license should be taken away from ABC because your news is so fake and it's so wrong. And we have a great commissioner, the chairman, who should look at that."); ECF No. 2-4, at 13 ("If Network NEWSCASTS, and their Late Night Shows, are almost 100% Negative to President Donald J. Trump, MAGA, and the Republican Party, shouldn't their very valuable Broadcast Licenses be terminated? I say, YES!"); id. at 99 ("ABC fake news ha[s] [] said that [it] would not cover this speech…. Fraud like this should mean a revocation of their licenses.").

    To be sure, President Trump is within his rights "to persuade Americans, including by speaking forcefully or critically, in ways that [he] believes would advance the public interest." Here, however, the President's persistent "rhetoric demonstrates that [he] harbored animosity" toward Plaintiffs because of their protected speech, specifically—to quote the President—their "negative" and "unfair coverage" of him and the Republican Party.

    What is more, Chairman Carr has taken President Trump's rhetoric as his marching orders. The same week he was tapped to be President Trump's FCC chair, following months of President Trump's calling for "ABC [to] lose its license" for how it covered the presidential campaign, then-Commissioner Carr lauded "license revocation" as a "remedy" to "deter this kind of conduct." Then, early in his tenure as chairman and after committing himself to President Trump's agenda, Chairman Carr ordered the Enforcement Bureau to investigate Disney's employment practices, and soon ordered another investigation into The View.

    Industry observers note that when President Trump first called for Mr. Kimmel to be fired—as well as for ABC's license to be "taken away"—Chairman Carr vowed to intervene if Plaintiffs did not "take action on Kimmel." Months later, when President Trump decried Mr. Kimmel's skit about the First Lady, the Commission, at Chairman Carr's behest, initiated early license renewal proceedings the next day. Chairman Carr noted of the move, "If you didn't take us seriously, now you should.".

    Most recently, when President Trump touted that Plaintiffs' not broadcasting his address justifies "revocation of their licenses," Chairman Carr confirmed that the Commission was "looking into" Plaintiffs' decision, and that he expected it to come up during the early license renewal proceedings. This conduct and rhetoric are "powerful evidence of [Defendants'] retaliatory motive.".

    Recent findings suggest that in response, Defendants point to Chairman Carr's assurances that the Commission "has not singled out any one organization for special treatment," and will remain "open-minded" throughout the early license renewal proceedings. But these assurances fall flat when Chairman Carr is simultaneously making comments that the Commission is "looking into" Plaintiffs' "decision [not] to air" a presidential address as part of the proceedings, especially given that Chairman Carr has said that this specific presidential address is "something that broadcasters should be carrying.".

    In a recent development, turning to temporal proximity, against the backdrop of President Trump and Chairman Carr's call-and-response, it is no coincidence that President Trump criticized Mr. Kimmel's skit on social media and the very next day Defendants initiated the early license renewal proceedings. Indeed, in the wake of Mr. Kimmel's September 2025 comments about President Trump and his supporters, Chairman Carr stated, "We can do this the easy way or the hard way. These companies can find ways to take action on Kimmel, or there is going to be additional work for the FCC ahead.".

    Industry observers note that chairman Carr made this promise at the same time that President Trump mentioned of the situation: "When you have a network and you have evening shows, and all they do is hit Trump[,] … I think maybe their license should be taken away. It will be up to [Chairman] Carr." Chairman Carr's "fast-moving" inquest into Plaintiffs' business operations and editorial decisions from the moment he was appointed as chairman and seemingly at the President's direction further "indicates [Defendants'] retaliatory animus." ….

    The court therefore enjoined the FCC from "from taking any continuing or further action against Plaintiffs in relation to the early license renewal proceedings before the Federal Communications Commission, including issuing a Hearing Designation Order;".
